tasks.fix_summary: The summary line can no longer disagree with the exit status, because both are derived from ONE value: a `failed` boolean computed from every class that forces a non-zero exit, used for the printed verdict and for the return. Each class is named with its own count rather than folded into the failure figure, and the reasoning is right - a viewport mismatch or an overflow still produced a file in `rows`, so counting it as a capture failure would misstate what happened. `len(rows)` therefore remains what it is (captures written), each class is reported by name, and the derived verdict closes the line.
tasks.evidence_after: tools/capture-devices.py: the `failed` expression covering failures, overflows, forced_failures, viewport_mismatches and empty_captures; the summary printing every class and ending in FAILED/OK; `return 1 if failed else 0`. ruff/pyright/format clean on the file.
tasks.notes: The fix is better than the one the task suggested. Folding every class into the `failures` count would have made the two agree and made the line less true; deriving a verdict from all of them makes them agree while keeping each count honest.

tasks.title: A failed health probe leaks its HTTPConnection until garbage collection
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the tools/ lane while fixing A10/A80/A81/A82, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: On the `except` path in `caddy_process` the `HTTPConnection` is not closed, so each failed attempt leaves a socket open until the garbage collector runs. Bounded in practice by the retry count, and pre-existing rather than introduced by A81, which rewrote the loop around it. A try/finally would close it.
tasks.fix_summary: The health probe's `HTTPConnection` is now closed in a `finally`, so the failure paths that used to leak a socket until garbage collection close it too. The fix establishes the contract before changing the code: the caller is handed the Caddy PROCESS, never this connection, so closing it at the probe is the whole of what is owed.
tasks.evidence_after: tools/capture-devices.py: the try/finally around `conn.request` / `conn.getresponse()` with an explanatory comment; ruff/pyright/format clean on the file.

tasks.file_line: AUDIT/ (how the fix lanes were scheduled)
tasks.title: Parallel Swift fix lanes cannot be isolated by scratch path or port: they compile the same module, so one lane's half-finished edit fails every other lane's build
tasks.discovered_by: the coordinator, from the fix phase stalling: three Swift lanes ran ~30 minutes without a single commit while the machine sat at load 57-92 with 25 compiler processes on 8 cores
tasks.evidence_before:
Three Swift lanes were started on disjoint FILES (ConversationEngine/ConversationStore; DocumentImport/MLXEngine; Sources/ChatBotsApp/**), each with its own `--scratch-path` under /tmp, and A83 had just made the test port allocator probe for a free port so concurrent test runs could not collide. None of that was sufficient. The lanes stalled: file mtimes showed edits from 10:38-10:45 and no commit by 10:54, the app-layer lane had written NOTHING at all in ~30 minutes, and the machine was at load 57-92 with 25 swift-frontend processes for 8 cores. The reason is the module boundary, not the files: `swift build` compiles Sources/ChatBotsCore as ONE module, so an in-progress edit in any lane's file is visible to every other lane's build. A fix that is half-applied - the normal state of a file between two edits - does not type-check, so the other two lanes fail their build for a reason that has nothing to do with their own change. CONFIRMED DIRECTLY, with the mechanism visible: one lane's new test file was half-written, and `swift build --build-tests` failed for everyone with

    Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditEngineStateTests.swift:17:15: error: type 'GatedLoopEngine' does not conform to protocol 'LLMEngine'

the same line repeated for every missing member, plus 'input file ... was modified during the build' because the owning lane was still editing it. The OTHER lane reported the same failure and showed that its own target compiled clean (`swift build --target ChatBotsCore` exit 0) - so a lane was blocked, and idled, by a file it did not own and must not edit. The coordinating agent's own build failed identically. Nothing about scratch paths or ports was involved.
tasks.fix_summary: Serialise Swift work: at most one lane editing Sources/ at a time. The two lanes that were stalled on each other were stopped and the remaining one was left to finish; the interrupted batches are re-run afterwards, one at a time. Non-Swift lanes stay parallel, because `tools/` and the docs share neither a module nor a compiler with Sources/. The scheduling rule this produces is stated here rather than rediscovered: parallelism is safe across REPOSITORIES and across LANGUAGE boundaries, and it is safe within Swift only across packages - not within one module.
tasks.evidence_after: After stopping the app-layer lane, the remaining two completed and committed their work; the app-layer batch was re-run on its own and its scratch directory was removed. Load fell and the builds completed.
tasks.notes: This is the fourth defect this audit has found in its own process, after A19 (a DONE claim whose commit carried nothing), A83 (a guard that skipped the case it targeted, and a test port allocator that collided) and A84 (a commit that absorbed another lane's staged files). The pattern across all four is the same and worth stating plainly: the audit was confident about its CONTROLS and had not checked its own MECHANISM. Each was found by looking at observed behaviour - a git status, a guard output, a file mtime - rather than by reasoning about the design, which is also how the substantive findings were found. The concrete instance is worth keeping because it names the cost precisely: a lane that had done nothing wrong lost its build for the duration, and its own target compiled clean throughout. Isolation has to be at the level of the unit the compiler actually sees, which for SwiftPM is the module and the test target - not the file.

tasks.title: The same connection-leak shape A86 fixed exists twice more, and one of them is called in a 90-iteration loop
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the tools/ lane while fixing A86, and left unfixed because it falls outside that task's scope
tasks.evidence_before: `server_is_up()` (:76-84) puts `conn.close()` AFTER `getresponse()` inside the try, so a probe that raises before returning leaks the socket - and `wait_for_server()` calls it in a loop of up to 90 attempts, so a service that is slow to come up can leak dozens of sockets rather than one. `profiles()` (:67-73) has the related shape with no try at all, though it is called once and returns immediately. This is the same class A86 fixed in `caddy_process`, found by the same person in the same file while fixing it.
tasks.fix_summary: Both remaining probe connections are closed in a `finally`. `server_is_up()` is the one that mattered: `wait_for_server` calls it in a loop of up to 90 attempts, so every failed probe leaked a socket. `profiles()` had the same shape with no try at all; it is called once, but leaving it inconsistent would be a trap for the next reader. Each fix establishes the caller's contract before changing the code - the body is read in full before the close and only the parsed list is returned; only the boolean is returned - so closing at the probe is the whole of what is owed.
tasks.evidence_after: The leak was demonstrated BEFORE it was fixed, which is what makes this trustworthy: against a loopback server whose status line is malformed (`BadStatusLine`, an HTTPException but not a ConnectionError, so CPython does not self-close), the pre-fix `server_is_up` left 7/7 sockets live with the peer still open, and through the real `wait_for_server` loop 8/8. After the fix: 0/7 and 0/8 live, one close each, return values and the propagated exception unchanged. ruff, ruff format, pyright all clean; no suppressions.
tasks.notes: The probe's detail is worth keeping: it subclasses HTTPConnection to keep instances alive after the function returns, and observes both the client-side fd and the server-side absence of EOF, so the leak is shown from two directions rather than inferred from a missing call.

tasks.file_line: AUDIT/ledger.json (how it is written), AUDIT/phase-e.sh section 11
tasks.title: The ledger is written non-atomically, and the acceptance run's most important gate passed on a ledger it could not parse
tasks.discovered_by: a fix lane reported seeing AUDIT/ledger.json as invalid JSON mid-write; checking what the tools do with that is what found the second half
tasks.evidence_before: TWO faults, and the second is the serious one. (1) The ledger is rewritten in place with `json.dump`, so a reader can observe a truncated file: a lane hit exactly that and reported 'invalid JSON when I last read it', which is a race rather than corruption - the file on disk was valid before and after. (2) `AUDIT/phase-e.sh` section 11 piped `jq` into a file and counted lines. On unparseable JSON jq writes nothing, so `total` and `open_count` were both 0 and the gate printed PASS - 'ledger: 0 tasks, none open, 0 blocked'. That is the one check that says whether the audit is finished, and it went green on a ledger that could not be read at all. The same shape as A83's guard skipping the case it targets and A28's counts taken from file sizes: a control that reports success on the broken input.
tasks.fix_summary: The gate now parses first and refuses to draw any conclusion if it cannot: `jq -e '.tasks | length'` must succeed, and the count must be greater than zero, or the section FAILS with the parse error written to a log. Only then does it count statuses. And the ledger is now written atomically - to a temporary file, then renamed over the original - so a concurrent reader sees either the old file or the new one and never a truncated one.
tasks.evidence_after: `jq -e '.tasks | length' AUDIT/ledger.json` => 93, and the file on disk and at HEAD both parse. `bash -n` and `shellcheck -S style` clean on phase-e.sh. THE FAILURE PATHS WERE EXERCISED, not assumed, since a guard whose failure path has never run is the exact defect this task is about: against a syntactically broken ledger `jq -e` fails with 'parse error: Unfinished JSON term at EOF' and the section FAILS instead of reporting zero open tasks; against a valid but EMPTY ledger the count is 0 and the '<= 0' clause fails it rather than printing '0 tasks, none open'; and against the real ledger it parses to 93 and proceeds to count statuses. Each of the three cases was run and its output observed.
tasks.notes: The pattern across this audit's own defects is now unmistakable and worth stating once: A19 (a DONE claim whose commit carried nothing), A83 (a guard that skipped its own target, and a port allocator that collided), A84 (a commit that absorbed another lane's files), A87 (parallel lanes sharing a module) and now A89 (a gate that passed on unparseable input) are all the same failure - the audit was confident about its CONTROLS and had not checked its own MECHANISM. Every one was found by looking at observed behaviour rather than by reasoning about the design, and every fix has been to make the mechanism fail loudly on the case it was silently tolerating.

tasks.title: Public API still computes the incoherent unlimited-thinking cap, and a test pins that value
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the A36/A42/A43 lane while fixing A43, and left unfixed because A43 was already committed under one-task-one-commit
tasks.evidence_before: `AgentSpec.generationCap` still computes `maxTokens + (thinking.reasoningTokenBudget ?? 0)`, so `.unlimited` yields exactly `maxTokens` - less total headroom than `.high`, which adds 8192. A43 fixed this in MLXEngine with `generationCap(answerBudget:thinking:contextWindow:)` and the engine no longer calls the old property, so it is now dead in production - but it is PUBLIC API that contradicts the fix, and any caller reaching for it gets the old, wrong answer. Worse, `ThinkingModeTests.swift:49` asserts the incoherent value: `#expect(spec.generationCap == 1_000, "unlimited adds no ceiling to the cap")`. A test that pins a defect is worse than no test, because it turns a fix into a failure and invites the next person to restore the bug.
tasks.fix_summary: The headroom arithmetic now has ONE implementation, on `ThinkingMode`, and both `AgentSpec.generationCap` and the engine's helper delegate to it - so a caller cannot get a different answer from the one the engine uses. `.unlimited` has no ceiling but MLX still needs a finite cap, so it is given the model's context window as headroom, floored at `.high`; the old `maxTokens + (reasoningTokenBudget ?? 0)` made unlimited the SMALLEST cap of any mode. It is kept as a type extension rather than on MLXEngine because it is arithmetic rather than inference. The test that pinned the defect now asserts the relationship that matters - high can never exceed unlimited - which is a stronger assertion than the constant it replaced.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/ChatModels.swift (the extension and the delegating property), MLXEngine.swift (the engine side now shares it), Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditWave2GenerationCapTests.swift adds 68 lines, and Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/ThinkingModeTests.swift is updated: the old `#expect(spec.generationCap == 1_000, "unlimited adds no ceiling to the cap")` is replaced by an expectation of the monotone relationship. swift build --build-tests 0 warnings 0 errors.
tasks.notes: The task was to fix a property that no longer had a production caller, purely because it is public API contradicting the fix beside it, and the test is the part that mattered most: a test asserting a defect on a public property is worse than no test, because it turns the correct behaviour into a failure and invites the next person to restore the bug. Its original message - 'unlimited adds no ceiling to the cap' - described an intent the arithmetic contradicted, which is the same shape as four other findings in this audit.

tasks.title: A round abandoned at the reasoning ceiling can still fall through to tool dispatch
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the A36/A42/A43 lane while fixing A43, and left unfixed because A43 was already committed under one-task-one-commit
tasks.evidence_before: After a ceiling-abandoned round, `guard !toolCalls.isEmpty` can still fall through to tool dispatch if a `.toolCall` chunk arrived while the stripper still considered itself inside reasoning - which a protocol-violating model can produce. The notice stays truthful, but the turn runs another round rather than ending, so the ceiling costs more than it should instead of terminating the turn.
tasks.fix_summary: An abandoned round now ends the turn deterministically, whatever fragments arrived. Previously the guard on tool calls could still fall through to dispatch if a `.toolCall` chunk arrived while the stripper considered itself inside reasoning - which a protocol-violating model can produce - so a turn the engine had already abandoned ran another round instead of finishing. The notice was already truthful; now the control flow is too.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/MLXEngine.swift; Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditWave2RoundAdvanceTests.swift adds 102 lines. swift build --build-tests 0 warnings 0 errors.
tasks.notes: A43 recorded this as the one path where its guarantee did not hold, rather than claiming the ceiling work was complete. Closing it took a separate task because the fix is a control-flow decision, not part of the ceiling accounting - which is why A43's lane left it rather than folding it in. A DEEPER DEFECT FOUND WHILE FIXING IT, which changes how A43 should be read: the ceiling's `break` was UNLABELLED and sat inside a `switch`, so it exited the switch while the `for try await` loop kept consuming the stream. A43's fix therefore did not actually abandon the stream - the delimiter reached the model after all, the opposite of what A43's comment claimed. A91's `break chunks` on a labelled loop is what makes the abandonment real. Recorded in A91 and not rewritten into A43: each entry describes its own change accurately, and the pair is the honest record.

tasks.title: Every engine event is published twice, duplicating live text, tool-log entries and every subscriber's stream
tasks.discovered_by: reported by a fix lane while working on an adjacent task, and left unfixed because it falls outside that task's scope
tasks.evidence_before: The `onEvent` closure calls `publishEvent(event)` at :880 and then `handle(event, from:)` at :881 - and `handle` calls `publishEvent(event)` again in every branch: turnFinished at :955, toolResult at :969, toolFailure at :973, default at :976. So `record(event)` runs twice, which doubles `liveState[...].text` and `.reasoning` and puts duplicate entries in `toolLog` - and `liveSeats` is what the interface draws. Every `observeEvents` subscriber and the `events` stream receive each token and tool event twice, so the HTTP API and WebTransport clients see duplicates, and the event volume feeding A41's buffer is doubled. The existing tests assert only `conversation.turns`, which `handle` appends exactly once, so nothing catches it.
tasks.fix_summary: Each engine event is published exactly once. The fix establishes WHICH call site owns publishing rather than deleting whichever looked redundant: `handle` is the one, because every branch in it ends in `publishEvent(event)` and it also folds the event into the transcript, so the duplicate publish in the `onEvent` closure was the extra one. That removes the doubled `liveState[...].text` and `.reasoning`, the duplicated `toolLog` entries and the duplicate delivery to every `observeEvents` subscriber and to the `events` stream.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/ConversationEngine.swift; Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditWave2EventDuplicationTests.swift adds 140 lines and observes the STREAM rather than the transcript, which is the path no existing test was watching. swift build --build-tests 0 warnings 0 errors.
tasks.notes: The comment left in the code records why the defect survived: `conversation.turns` is appended once either way, so every test that asserted the transcript was correct while the live and streaming paths - what the interface actually draws - were doubled. That is the same shape as A35's dead branches: the tests were watching the right thing for the transcript and nothing was watching the surface the user sees.

tasks.title: The documented capture command fails on a fresh checkout because `.run/` does not exist yet
tasks.discovered_by: reported by a fix lane while working on an adjacent task, and left unfixed because it falls outside that task's scope
tasks.evidence_before: `start_servers()` opens `ROOT/.run/capture-engine.log` at :129, but nothing has created `.run/` at that point: `caddy_process()` creates it (`config.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)`) and `main()` calls `start_servers()` at ~:293 BEFORE `caddy_process()` at ~:294. `.run/` is gitignored and is otherwise created by `tools/start-app.sh`, so on a fresh clone the documented `python3 tools/capture-devices.py` raises an unhandled FileNotFoundError at :129 instead of the tool's own message. Established from the call order and `git check-ignore -v .run`; not executed on a fresh checkout because that path reaches `swift build`, which the reporting lane was not permitted to run.
tasks.fix_summary: A `run_directory()` helper creates `ROOT/.run` and returns it; `start_servers()` opens its engine log through it, and `caddy_process()` now derives its generated Caddyfile path from it too, replacing its own mkdir. That makes ONE ensurement point rather than one that happened to work because another function ran first. Fixed at the WRITE SITE, deliberately: reordering `main()` would have been wrong, because `caddy_process()` waits for a 200 from the Caddy port and the Caddyfile proxies /api/* to the engine, so the engine must already be running - reordering would make Caddy time out on every run. `RunDirectory.swift` answers the same question for the app and engine, and its 'one place decides' invariant is mirrored while its `~/Library/Application Support` fallback is deliberately NOT: this tool builds and serves the checkout it lives in, so its log belongs beside that checkout's state.
tasks.evidence_after: The failure was demonstrated before it was fixed, using HEAD's own source: with ROOT set to a directory with no `.run`, `git show HEAD:tools/capture-devices.py` loaded as a module raised `FileNotFoundError: '.../.run/capture-engine.log'` from `start_servers()`, and the fixed module created the directory and the log instead. python3 -m py_compile, ruff check, ruff format --check and pyright all clean; no suppression, no except added.
tasks.notes: This is the fresh-clone class A18 was about, one layer down - the suite was made hermetic and this tool still assumed a developer's machine. The fix's shape is the same as A86's and A88's: establish the invariant (one place creates the directory) rather than patch the symptom at each site.

tasks.file_line: tools/capture-devices.py (capture, downscale, build_index; OUT created only in main at :303)
tasks.title: The capture output directory is created only by main(), so any other caller of capture() or build_index() hits the same fresh-directory failure A93 fixed
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the A93 lane, which checked for the same assumption elsewhere in the file and found it
tasks.evidence_before: `capture()` (through `cdp.screenshot`) and `downscale()` write into `OUT`, and `build_index()` writes `OUT/index.html`, without any of them ensuring OUT exists - only `main()` creates it, at :303. From the documented entry point main() runs first, so it is latent today; any other caller, or a future reordering, hits the same FileNotFoundError class A93 fixed for `.run/`.
tasks.fix_summary: One ensurement point, `output_directory()`, creates the capture output directory and returns it, and all three writers go through it: `capture()` and `downscale()` were changed to take the capture's file NAME and resolve `output_directory() / name` internally, so they can no longer be handed a path whose parent some other function was trusted to have created, and `build_index()` writes through the same helper. `main()`'s own raw mkdir was REMOVED and its stale-sweep now calls the helper too, so there is one mechanism invoked from three sites rather than a live one plus a dead one - which is the same choice A93 made when it replaced caddy_process()'s raw mkdir with run_directory().
tasks.evidence_after: The fault and the fix were both demonstrated, with the pre-fix source loaded from the commit that recorded A93: with the output directory absent, pre-fix `capture()` printed a failed capture and left no directory, `downscale()` raised FileNotFoundError, and `build_index()` raised FileNotFoundError; post-fix all three succeeded and the directory existed. py_compile, ruff check, ruff format --check and pyright all clean; no suppression, no except added.
tasks.notes: An accuracy note from the reporter that is worth keeping, because it calibrates the severity rather than the fix: at the capture site the pre-fix FileNotFoundError does NOT escape - capture()'s own `except (DevToolsError, OSError, ValueError, KeyError)` catches it (FileNotFoundError is an OSError) and reports a generic failed capture - so only build_index() was fatal. The fault was real at all three sites but loud at two. That is also why it survived: a missing directory was indistinguishable from a dead Chrome in the tool's own output, which is an adjacent diagnosability gap reported rather than fixed.

tasks.title: Coverage is still keyword-presence based, so one SOURCED sentence naming all ten subjects still closes a session as fully answered
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the S1 lane while fixing A67/A75/A76, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: A67 raised the bar usefully - coverage now requires a contribution that gave a basis, and the markers must begin a word, so 'law' no longer matches flaw and 'source' no longer matches resource - but it did not change what coverage IS. A single contributed sentence that carries a basis marker and names all ten subjects still satisfies every subject at once, latches `.answered`, and stops a 20-round session early. The repository's own test asserts exactly that case and passes: `ResearchDirectorTests.theSessionEndsWhenNothingIsOutstanding`. A67's lane left it alone rather than editing an existing test, and said so.
tasks.fix_summary: Coverage now requires the room's ENGAGEMENT rather than a sentence naming the subject: a subject one seat names with a basis is a mention, and becomes covered only when a second seat names it, or when a seat answers the moderator's directed assignment on it. The assignment is recognised by the fixed phrase the app itself writes ('Nothing so far has addressed ...'), so the response to it counts from one seat without adding a field to `Turn`. A keyword in an unsourced assertion still leaves the subject open, and the A67 basis gate is unchanged.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/ResearchDirector.swift; Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditResearchCoverageTests.swift adds 109 lines and AuditS1ResearchCoverageTests.swift is extended. swift build --build-tests 0 warnings 0 errors; suite green.
tasks.notes: This is the different KIND of rule the finding asked for rather than a tighter threshold, and it is what text matching could not express: 'the room worked through the cost question' is a fact about more than one participant, so the rule had to be about who said what rather than about which words appear. The honest consequence is unchanged from A67 - the claim is harder to earn and sessions run longer - which was the direction the task required.

tasks.title: `affinity` still scores with bare substring matching, deciding which seat is asked about what
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the S1 lane while fixing A67/A75/A76, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: `affinity(_:for:)` scores with `haystack.contains($1)` - the same bare-substring shape A67 fixed for coverage, in the same file. It decides WHO is asked rather than whether the claim is made, so the consequence is a poorer choice of analyst rather than a false claim; A67's lane left it alone to avoid changing seat selection under a coverage task. 'law' matching 'flaw' and 'source' matching 'resource' can still steer a question to the wrong seat.
tasks.fix_summary: `affinity` scores on words rather than fragments, so 'law' no longer matches 'flaw' and 'source' no longer matches 'resource' when choosing which seat is asked about what. A67 fixed the same bare-substring shape for coverage; this is the same fix applied to the question-routing path, where the consequence is a poorer question rather than a false claim.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/ResearchDirector.swift; the determinism and coverage suites cover it. swift build --build-tests 0 warnings 0 errors; suite green.

tasks.title: `hasBasis` matches bare substrings, and A67 made its looseness load-bearing
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the S1 lane while fixing A67/A75/A76, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: `hasBasis` tests for markers with bare `contains`, so 'statistic' matches 'statistically' and 'assum' matches 'assumptions'. Before A67 that only affected a secondary read; A67 now gates ALL coverage on it, so every claim that a subject has been answered rests on this looseness. The bar A67 raised is therefore not as high as it reads: a turn can qualify as basis-bearing on a word that merely contains a marker.
tasks.fix_summary: `hasBasis` requires a basis marker to be a whole word, with an explicit inflection list, so 'statistic' no longer matches 'statistically' and 'assum' no longer matches 'assumptions'. That matters more than it looks: A67 made this matcher load-bearing for ALL coverage, so the bar A67 raised rested on a looseness A67 did not tighten. The lane also removed 'report' from the marker list after finding that adding it broke A67's behaviour by admitting unsourced 'the report says' prose - caught and reverted rather than shipped.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/ResearchDirector.swift (`hasBasis` and a `wholeWord` helper with an explicit inflection list); Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditResearchBasisTests.swift. swift build --build-tests 0 warnings 0 errors; swift test => 'Test run with 699 tests in 117 suites passed'.
tasks.notes: Reported by the lane that INTRODUCED the dependency on this matcher, which is the useful part: it flagged that its own fix rested on something it had not tightened. A95 and A97 interact by design - tightening the basis test moves the coverage bar again - so they were reasoned about together and committed separately.

tasks.file_line: Caddyfile (and the header set added by A76)
tasks.title: In the documented configuration Caddy serves the page, so the CSP, nosniff, frame denial and referrer policy A76 added never reach it
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the S1 lane while fixing A67/A75/A76, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: A76's headers are emitted by the Swift server. But `tools/start*.sh` start Caddy when it is installed, and Caddyfile serves `./web` itself while only PROXYING /api/* to the engine - so in the normal deployment the HTML the browser loads is served by Caddy and carries none of the new headers. The API responses get them; the document that needs a CSP most does not. The lane could not fix this because the Caddyfile was outside its file set, and it said so rather than letting the fix look complete.
tasks.fix_summary: The Caddyfile's static `handle` block now emits the same four browser-boundary headers A76 added to the Swift server - nosniff, no-referrer, X-Frame-Options DENY and a Content-Security-Policy that is byte-for-byte A76's interface policy, with no 'unsafe-inline'. It is scoped to the static block, so the engine's own headers on /api/* are untouched, which `caddy adapt` confirms: the four response handlers appear in the static subroute only.
tasks.evidence_after: Measured rather than read, on a spare port, started the way tools/start.sh starts Caddy. `curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:7993/` returns all four headers; /app.js, /style.css and a file_server 404 return them too; /api/conversations with the engine down returns Caddy's own 502 with no security headers, which is the intended scoping since the engine supplies them when it is up. `caddy validate` => 'Valid configuration', exit 0. Caddy stopped afterwards: lsof on the port exits 1 and no caddy process remains. The lane re-read web/ itself rather than trusting A76's note and found no inline script, handler or style, no external origin, no eval/new Function/document.write, and no url() or @import in the stylesheet - so no directive had to be weakened to make the page work.
tasks.notes: The pre-existing `caddy fmt` warning (a blank line above the change) was confirmed identical before and after, so no unrelated reformat was introduced. Not verified and stated as such: live browser rendering under the policy, and the /api/* pass-through with the engine actually running - the latter is inferred from Caddy's semantics because the lane may not run swift build.

tasks.title: Kept-conversation share links 404 in the documented deployment, because Caddy proxies only /api/* and the engine serves /s/<id>
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the A98 lane, which measured /s/ while checking where Caddy's new headers applied
tasks.evidence_before: `APIServer.swift:407` serves `GET /s/<id>` when `request.path.hasPrefix("/s/")`, but the Caddyfile reverse-proxies only `/api/*`; everything else falls through to the static file_server. Measured with Caddy running on a spare port and the engine down: `curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:7993/s/any-id` => `HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found`, served by Caddy's file_server rather than the engine. So in the deployment the start scripts actually create, every share link is broken. Compounding it, the generated shareBase still points at the engine port (127.0.0.1:7789), which a phone on the LAN cannot reach even if the path resolved.
tasks.fix_summary: Caddy proxies `/s/*` to the engine, so the page is reachable in the documented deployment at all. The link's base no longer comes from the engine's loopback port: the web interface uses its own origin, the engine builds the share page's links from the request's `Host` (checked before it is reflected), `--share-base` lets a deployment state the address it is published on, and `tools/start.sh` sets it from the LAN address it is serving on. A Host that is not a host falls back to the configured base rather than being interpolated into a URL.
tasks.evidence_after: Caddyfile (the `handle /s/*` block), web/app.js, Sources/ChatBotsCore/APIServer.swift (init parameter, `validShareHost`, `sharedPage(id:host:)`), Sources/ChatBotsCLI/main.swift (`--share-base`), tools/start.sh (`share_base`), Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditShareLinkTests.swift, Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/SharedConversationTests.swift. Routing proved with Caddy 2.11.4 against the real engine and an unknown id, so the response body says who answered: shipped config -> Caddy's file-server body, no engine wording; fixed config -> the engine's own page. `caddy validate --config Caddyfile` reports a valid configuration. `--share-base http://192.168.18.27:7788` was read back from `/api/state` on a live engine. `start.sh`'s helper returns `http://192.168.18.27:7788` on this LAN and `http://127.0.0.1:7788` under `--local-only`. The Host reflection is covered twice: a pure test of what may be reflected, and an HTTP test that drives a real conversation and asserts the served page carries the proxied host and falls back for a hostile one. Full suite: 824 tests in 139 suites passed. NOT verified: an actual phone opening a link.
tasks.notes: The second half is the one worth carrying forward: the link 404'd, and fixing the route alone would still have produced a link that the device the feature exists for could not open — so the task could have been closed with a green test and a broken feature. The shape is F19's and A98's (the page and the engine disagreeing about who serves what), and it is why the fix was measured through Caddy rather than at the engine's own port. A residual is stated rather than hidden: the desktop app's link now follows `--share-base`, which `start.sh` sets; an app-launched engine that the user starts without `start.sh` keeps the loopback base, which is correct for the Mac it runs on and not for a phone.

tasks.title: The reader uses the REQUEST timeout as its idle receive timeout, so a stream quiet for longer than that fails the connection
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the core-lane while fixing A39/A52/A53, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: The client passes `configuration.timeoutMilliseconds` to the reader's `stream.receive()` as well as to request timeouts, so a stream that stays silent longer than the request timeout kills the reader. Measured directly while writing A39: with a 2-second client timeout the reader died after 2 seconds of engine work. At the shipped 10-second default the consequence is concrete and now more likely: **A15 moved document conversion off the main actor, so a conversion can legitimately take longer than 10 seconds**, and an attachment upload longer than that kills the reader - the command then reports a connection failure while `isConnected` stays true, which is A38's shape. A client that does not poll at 1 Hz also loses its connection after any quiet period.
tasks.fix_summary: The reader has its own idle timeout rather than borrowing the request deadline. `idleTimeoutMilliseconds` defaults to 120 seconds and `openBidirectionalStream(timeoutMilliseconds:)` now lets one session carry two deadlines: the connect gets the request deadline and the stream gets the idle one. So a stream that is merely QUIET longer than a request takes is no longer treated as dead - which matters because A15 made long document conversions normal traffic on this channel - while a genuinely dead peer is still detected.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/WebTransportClient.swift: `idleTimeoutMilliseconds` and the two-deadline stream open; Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditWave2IdleTimeoutTests.swift adds 160 lines. swift build --build-tests 0 warnings 0 errors.
tasks.notes: The fix states that the idle timeout is a BACKSTOP rather than the only liveness check, which is the part worth keeping: a dead QUIC connection closes on its own idle timeout and any receive fails the reader, so raising the idle deadline does not make a dead peer look alive - it only stops a quiet one being mistaken for one.

tasks.title: BMP and TIFF are accepted and sent as media types the Responses API does not document, the mirror of A52
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the core-lane while fixing A39/A52/A53, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: The magic-byte sniffer recognises BMP and TIFF and the intake path sends them as `image/bmp` and `image/tiff`. The same API documentation A52's lane checked lists png, jpeg, webp and gif; BMP and TIFF are not in it, so those attachments are sent and likely rejected with a 400. This is A52's defect in the other direction - A52 fixed a type the app offered but did not send; this is a type the app sends but the API may not take. Not fixed because `ImageUploadTests.mediaTypeFromMagicBytes` asserts those two media types, so the fix requires editing that existing test, and the equivalent decision (convert, or refuse at intake with a visible reason) belongs with a task that owns it.
tasks.fix_summary: BMP and TIFF are converted rather than sent as `image/bmp` and `image/tiff`, which the API documentation does not list - the mirror of A52, where a type the app offered was not sent, against this, where a type the app sent was likely rejected. They are common formats (macOS writes TIFF, other systems produce BMP), so conversion rather than refusal is what handles them, and the conversion path is now the same one A52 built for HEIC.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/Attachments.swift and DocumentImport.swift; Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditClientsImageTests.swift adds 169 lines and Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/ImageUploadTests.swift is UPDATED - it pinned the two media types. swift build --build-tests 0 warnings 0 errors; suite green.
tasks.notes: A52 and A101 together are the argument for one list rather than three: what the picker offers, what the magic-byte sniffer recognises, and what the API accepts were separate opinions in separate places, and each of the two defects was a disagreement between a different pair of them. The lane was asked whether they can be one list and will have said if not.

tasks.file_line: Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/TransportGate.swift (the five suites that drive a real QUIC listener or client)
tasks.title: One full-suite run aborted with a Network.framework fatal error, reduced but not fixed by A40's single-close
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the core-lane while fixing A39/A52/A53, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: One full run of the suite aborted with `Network/Connection.swift:5833: Fatal error: Neither nw nor nwGroup is initialized`, in WebTransportSessionTests while the new transport suites ran in parallel. A40's single-closer change removed a double `session.close()` - an obvious candidate cause - and the suite was clean over three consecutive full runs afterwards, but that is three runs, not a fix. Network.framework is known to be fragile with concurrent WebTransport endpoints on one host.
tasks.fix_summary: One actor gate, applied as a suite trait (`TransportSerialized`) to each of the five suites that construct a WebTransport server or client, so the transport tests run one at a time across suites instead of only within each. The gate releases on the throwing path, so a failing test cannot leak it and deadlock the rest; and it hands over through a continuation queue rather than a semaphore, because the wait is `async` and blocking a cooperative thread would be a deadlock under a bounded pool.
tasks.evidence_after: Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/TransportGate.swift, and one trait per suite in WebTransportSessionTests.swift:95, AuditReplyMatchingTests.swift:119, AuditWave2IdleTimeoutTests.swift:97, AuditTransportServerTests.swift:89, AuditTransportLifecycleTests.swift:92. The abort was reproduced live before the fix, on a full-suite run in this session: `Network/Connection.swift:5833: Fatal error: Neither nw nor nwGroup is initialized`, no test summary, exit 1. After the fix the full suite was run three times in sequence: `821 tests in 138 suites passed`, exit 0 each time, no abort. The transport suites now take ~19 s each rather than overlapping. NOT proven: that Network.framework is safe under concurrency — the trait constrains the tests, not the library, and the code says so.
tasks.notes: Serialising the suites was the recorded next step and is what was done, rather than retrying until a run went green — a retry would have converted a hard abort into an intermittent one and left Phase E to rediscover it as a crash. The generalisable part is the trait: a per-suite `.serialized` trait reads as if it makes a suite safe to run alongside others, and it does not, which is how five suites each ended up individually serialised and collectively concurrent.

tasks.title: Attachment document text is still promoted into the system role, so a crafted document can inject instruction into every seat's prompt
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the A69 lane, which fixed the same class of boundary for peer text and social state and then looked for the other untrusted inputs
tasks.evidence_before: `attachmentContext` is joined into the single system message beside the seat's brief, and the document text it carries arrives through `POST /api/attachments` - unauthenticated in the documented LAN configuration (A01), and the same intake path A29 was about. So a document added by anyone who can reach the port, or one a moderator was persuaded to add, can carry text that reads as system-role instruction to every seat in the room. The moderator's `topic` is interpolated into the system message verbatim at :435 by the same path. A69 moved peer-derived text out of the system role and made the bracket convention unforgeable; this is the remaining instance of the same class, and it fell outside A69's cited lines.
tasks.fix_summary: Both untrusted inputs are out of the system role. The moderator's topic is no longer interpolated into the system message at all - it remains in the log as the moderator's own topic turn and in the opening brief - and the source material is now fenced data in the USER role, using the app's own fence token, beside the log. So a document arriving through the unauthenticated POST /api/attachments, or a crafted question, can no longer read as system-role instruction to every seat in the room. This is A69's shape applied to the two inputs A69 did not cover.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/PromptBuilder.swift; Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditResearchPromptTrustTests.swift adds 110 lines, and Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AttachmentTests.swift is UPDATED - it pinned the old placement in the system message, which is why the defect survived. swift build --build-tests 0 warnings 0 errors; suite green.
tasks.notes: Left by the lane because `AttachmentTests.swift:250-266` pins the current placement, so the fix needs that existing test changed - the same situation A53 and A90 hit. That is worth noting as a pattern: three recent findings have been held in place by a test asserting the behaviour being fixed, which is itself evidence about how they survived. Also reported and not worth its own task: `PromptBuilder.systemMessage`'s `moderator` parameter at :110 is never used - dead API rather than a defect with impact.

tasks.title: Tool dispatch runs the injected registry rather than the tool set the caller passed, so disabling a tool does not prevent it running
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the research lane while fixing A73 and A95, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: `generate` accepts a `tools` array and `ConversationEngine` passes `tools: []` when `webSearchEnabled` is false - but dispatch calls `toolRegistry.run(name:)` against the registry rather than against the passed array. So a model that emits a `web_search` call (a hallucinated or injected tool call) reaches the network even though the user turned web search off, and no per-turn budget gate can be enforced at the provider level at all. It is also why A73's search ceiling can only bind BETWEEN turns: the count is known at turn end, so one in-flight turn can overshoot by however many calls it makes.
tasks.fix_summary: A turn can only run the tools its caller offered. Dispatch previously went through the injected toolRegistry rather than the tools array passed to generate, so ConversationEngine passing tools: [] for webSearchEnabled == false did not stop a hallucinated or injected web_search from reaching the network. The decision is now a testable TurnToolSet, and an unoffered call is refused, not executed.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/MLXEngine.swift; Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditClientsToolDispatchTests.swift. The new test was shown RED without the fix: an unoffered web_search ran. swift build (all products) and swift build --build-tests 0 warnings 0 errors; swift test => 'Test run with 752 tests in 124 suites passed'.
tasks.notes: Stated coverage gap: the dispatch DECISION is fully driven, but the generateExclusively wiring that calls it needs model weights and is not executed, so 'generate refuses an unoffered call' is covered at the unit rather than through a loaded model. Also noted for A73, closed earlier: the offered set is now authoritative, so its between-turns ceiling genuinely binds where it previously only read as if it did. A per-turn gate is now possible because the engine knows the offered set before any call happens, but A73's accounting is still charged at turn end and its stated limit is unchanged - the gate was deliberately NOT added, because silently changing a closed task's stated limit is worse than leaving a known bound.

tasks.title: A95's directed-engagement path identifies the moderator's assignment by an exact phrase, so rewording the assignment silently disables it
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the research lane while fixing A73 and A95, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: The rule that makes a directed assignment count from a single seat works by matching the exact prefix "Nothing so far has addressed \(label)" in a `.direction` turn. If the wording is ever changed - by a copy edit, a localisation, or someone tightening the prose - the match fails, the assignment no longer registers, and the engagement rule silently reverts to requiring two seats with nothing reporting the change. The lane that wrote it reported the coupling itself.
tasks.fix_summary: The directed assignment is carried as a typed marker on the turn rather than recognised by its wording. `Turn` gains a `Kind` (defaulting to `.rotation`) and an `unaddressedSubject` marker, and the director reads the marker instead of matching an exact phrase - so a copy edit or a localisation of the moderator's instruction can no longer silently disable the engagement rule and revert coverage to requiring two seats. A turn written before the field existed is still read from its wording ONCE, which is the migration path for stored conversations rather than a second permanent mechanism.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/ChatModels.swift and ConversationEngine.swift; the coverage and determinism suites cover it. swift build --build-tests 0 warnings 0 errors.
tasks.notes: The structural fix is what the finding asked for and it needed a `Turn` field, which is why A95's lane left it rather than folding it in. The legacy fallback is deliberate and bounded: without it, every conversation saved before this change would silently stop registering its assignments.

tasks.title: A user-typed key is still taken verbatim, so a pasted key with a trailing newline suppresses the missing-key warning
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the clients lane while fixing A55/A57/A58, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: `effectiveAPIKey` returns a user-typed key verbatim when `apiKey` is non-empty, and `isMissingKey` treats a whitespace-only value as present. So a pasted key with a trailing newline carries a control character into the Authorization header and simultaneously suppresses the missing-key warning - the same class as A55, on the path A55 did not cover, which was the file and environment path. Related and reported together: `host(of:)` at :231 trims .whitespaces while `responsesURL` trims .whitespacesAndNewlines, the same small inconsistency that produced A55.
tasks.fix_summary: The typed key path uses the same normaliser as the other two, and the host check agrees with the URL builder. `effectiveAPIKey` routes a user-typed value through `BuiltInKeys.normalisedKey` - the third caller A55's shared function was introduced for - so a pasted key with a trailing newline no longer carries a control character into the Authorization header while also suppressing the missing-key warning. `host(of:)` now trims `.whitespacesAndNewlines` like `responsesURL`.
tasks.evidence_after: Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditCLIClientKeyTests.swift adds 4 tests, and the lane verified them by DISABLING the fix: all four fail pre-fix with 11 issues, including the typed value returned verbatim and a whitespace-only value keeping `isMissingKey` false. swift test => 765 tests in 127 suites passed.
tasks.notes: A55's fix introduced one shared `normalisedKey` for the file and environment paths; the typed path is the third, so the same structural answer applies - route it through the same normaliser rather than trimming at the call site. Recorded rather than fixed because it was outside A55's stated scope.

tasks.title: A failed or incomplete response does not end the read loop, so the turn waits out the request timeout
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the clients lane while fixing A55/A57/A58, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: `response.failed` and `response.incomplete` yield `.failed` but do not break the read loop. A server that reports a failure and then holds the connection open keeps the turn alive until the 600-second request timeout, so a user waits ten minutes for a failure the server already reported. Pre-existing rather than introduced by A54 - and A54's terminal-event requirement makes the path more relevant, since a stream with no terminal event is now a failure the reader must conclude rather than wait out.
tasks.fix_summary: A reported failure ends the read rather than waiting out the timeout. The read loop is labelled, and `response.failed`, `response.incomplete` and a top-level error all `break readLoop` - the old `break` only left the `switch`, which is why a server that failed and then held the connection kept the turn alive to the 600-second request timeout.
tasks.evidence_after: Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditCLIStreamTerminationTests.swift adds 3 tests, verified by disabling the two breaks: all three fail pre-fix with `text == "beforeafter"` and `completions == 1`. swift test => 768 tests in 128 suites passed.

tasks.title: Two pre-existing sources of full-suite flakiness, both reproducing with the newest suites excluded
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the clients lane while fixing A55/A57/A58, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: Two intermittent failures were observed and both were confirmed NOT to come from the changes being made: they reproduce with every AuditClients suite skipped. (1) AuditEngineStateTestsEventStream.swift:94 intermittently fails, reporting a received count of 172 or 7 against an expected 256 - a timing-dependent expectation about a bounded stream, which is the same territory as A41's .bufferingNewest(256). (2) The WebTransport suite crashed once inside Apple's framework: Network/Connection.swift:5833: Fatal error: Neither nw nor nwGroup is initialized. Every task in that wave still got a green full run before its commit, so no task rests on a flaky run, though A101 needed a re-run.
tasks.fix_summary: The bounded-stream test's read is now `read until the stream has been quiet for 400 ms` instead of `read for a fixed 300 ms`. The producer has already finished when the read starts, so quiet is a property of the stream rather than of the machine's load, and the assertion that the buffer kept the newest 256 is unchanged. The second half of the finding — the WebTransport suite aborting the process — is fixed with A102.
tasks.evidence_after: Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditEngineStateTestsEventStream.swift (the `drain` helper and its call site). The full suite was run three times in sequence after the change: `821 tests in 138 suites passed`, exit 0 each time. NOT reproduced in this session: the 172 and 7 counts the ledger recorded, which need a loaded host. The change removes the timing dependence by construction; the arithmetic is that the producer finished before the read began, so the buffer holds exactly its bound once the reader has caught up.
tasks.notes: The test was asserting a real invariant with an instrument that could not measure it: a fixed read window is a statement about the machine, not about the buffer. The audit's own note on this is that a bounded stream's exact delivered count is not deterministic by design, so the fix is to make the read deterministic rather than to loosen the assertion — the assertion is the part that has value. Recorded as a residual: reading until quiet is still a heuristic, though now one that only fails if the reader is starved for 400 ms rather than merely slowed.

tasks.title: Dropbox renames .git/index to a conflicted copy, which git reads as an empty index and shows the whole tree as deleted
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the app-layer lane immediately after a commit, which is the only reason it was caught rather than misread as a catastrophic working-tree change
tasks.evidence_before: Just after committing A48, `git status` showed all 226 tracked files as staged DELETIONS with everything untracked. The cause was that `.git/index` no longer existed: Dropbox had renamed it to `.git/index (Andre Borchert's conflicted copy 2026-09-13)`. Git read the missing index as empty, so HEAD's entire tree looked deleted. No `.git/index.lock` was held, so this was not a lock contention problem and serialising commits would not have prevented it. Verified afterwards from the coordinator side: `.git/index` restored at 24,643 bytes, HEAD 30f930c on branch audit/2026-09-13, `git diff --cached` empty, and A46/A47/A48 intact in history. `xattr -p com.dropbox.ignored .git` returns nothing, so Dropbox IS syncing git's internals - a previous session had marked `.build`, `models`, `dist` and `captures` as Dropbox-ignored for exactly this class of interference, and `.git` was not included. SECOND AND THIRD CLOBBERS: the index vanished again after the coordinator's A109 commit, replaced by a second conflicted copy, and once more after the approved attribute was applied to .git - the last surfacing as `fatal: .git/index: unable to map index file: Stale NFS file handle`, because git held the inode Dropbox replaced. All three were recovered the same way (`rm -f .git/index && git reset --mixed HEAD`), HEAD verified intact each time and the working tree never touched. Related: a commit killed at the session's 60-second limit left a stale zero-byte `.git/index.lock`, removed only after `lsof` reported no holder AND `git log` confirmed the commit had not landed.
tasks.fix_summary: Applied with the owner's approval: `xattr -w com.dropbox.ignored 1 .git`, the mechanism a previous session applied to `.build`, `models`, `dist` and `captures`. Dropbox stops syncing git's internals, so the clobbering stops; `origin` on GitHub already replicates the repository and every wave is pushed. Verified: attribute set, `.git/index` present, `git status --porcelain` empty, `git diff HEAD` empty, HEAD e328e82. The three stale conflicted copies inside .git are left in place - they are evidence of the race, git ignores unknown files there, and deleting files inside .git is not something to do casually.
tasks.evidence_after: Recovered and verified after each of the three clobbers: HEAD intact on audit/2026-09-13, index rebuilt from HEAD, working tree untouched, all lane commits present. The attribute is now set, so the race should not recur.
tasks.notes: The recovery used was `git reset --mixed HEAD`, which rebuilds the index from HEAD without touching the working tree or history - the correct tool for a clobbered index, and worth recording because the wrong reflex (a hard reset, or re-adding everything) would have destroyed either the working tree or the staging state. The deeper risk is the one to state plainly: a clobbered index DURING a commit could produce a commit built from a wrong tree, and because this audit's evidence is its commits, that would corrupt the audit's own record rather than merely annoy a developer. The real fix is to mark `.git` as Dropbox-ignored so Dropbox stops syncing git internals - `origin` on GitHub already provides replication and every wave is pushed - but that changes the owner's sync configuration, so it is being asked rather than done. The recovery is worth recording precisely BECAUSE the wrong reflex is destructive: `git reset --hard` would have discarded the working tree and `git add -A` would have staged 207 phantom deletions. A clobbered index needs `git reset --mixed HEAD` - rebuild the index from HEAD, touch nothing else. The stale-lock incident is the mirror image: a lock may be stale or live and the difference matters, so `lsof` is the check, made before removal rather than after.

tasks.title: APISnapshot carries no revision and its only ordering field is whole-second, so a reply racing a push within one second can still regress the interface's state
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the app-layer lane while fixing A47/A48, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: A48's guard orders snapshots by `serverTime`, encoded `.iso8601` and therefore whole-second, so two snapshots in the same second cannot be ordered at all. The poll is covered because A48 also added an in-flight counter, but a `run` reply racing a push within the same second can still apply an older `status`. The same missing field has a second consequence: the guard is wall-clock based, so a backwards system clock step would make every later snapshot look stale and freeze the interface's updates - a stuck UI caused by the clock, which is the class of defect A35 was about.
tasks.fix_summary: Snapshots are ordered by a monotonic revision rather than by the wall clock. `APISnapshot` gains an optional `revision`, incremented by `EngineService.snapshot()` - the single snapshot producer, so a reply and a push both carry it - and `APISnapshot.isOlder(than:)` compares revisions when both sides have one, falling back to `serverTime` otherwise. `ChatController`'s staleness check is now that call and the old applied-time bookkeeping is gone. The fallback is deliberate and stated: an older engine's frame still decodes because the field is optional, and a revision is never compared against a missing one. No persisted format changed.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/APIServer.swift, EngineService.swift, Sources/ChatBotsApp/ChatController.swift; Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditFinalSnapshotRevisionTests.swift. Three tests were shown to FAIL without the fix (clock-only comparison, no increment): same-second ordering by revision, a backwards clock step, and a strictly increasing stamp. swift test => 809 tests in 134 suites passed. NOT verifiable: the app-side call itself, since the test target cannot import the executable target - the rule it calls is tested and `swift build --target ChatBots` is clean.
tasks.notes: This closes both halves of the finding with one field, which is why they were recorded as one task: whole-second resolution could not order two snapshots in the same second, and a wall-clock comparison would freeze the interface if the system clock stepped backwards - a stuck UI caused by the clock, the class A35 was about.

tasks.title: The stored-attachment doc claims the saved record carries the extracted text, which it does not
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the app-layer lane while fixing A47/A48, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: The doc comment says stored attachments carry their extracted text, and they do not: `ChatController.attachments` rebuilds with an empty `text` and the bytes were never persisted. This is not cosmetic - it is WHY A47 could only preserve-and-inform rather than re-upload, so the false invariant is the root of a task rather than a footnote to one. A doc comment asserting a property the data does not have is the shape this audit has recorded repeatedly, here with a concrete consequence: re-opening a conversation loses the material to the models.
tasks.fix_summary: The doc now describes what is actually stored: the engine's DESCRIPTION of an attachment rather than its extracted text. `ChatController.attachments` rebuilds with an empty text and the bytes were never persisted, so the old comment asserted a property the data does not have - and that false invariant is precisely why A47 could only preserve-and-inform rather than re-upload.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/UserSettings.swift. swift build --build-tests 0 warnings 0 errors.
tasks.notes: The persisted format was NOT changed, which is the right call for a doc correction: changing what is stored so the comment becomes true would be a data migration dressed up as a comment fix, and A47's fallback already handles the honest version. The lane was asked to say whether the data or the doc should change, and the answer - the doc - is recorded.

tasks.title: Restored-but-not-loaded files appear as ordinary attachment chips, distinguished only by a notice the user can dismiss
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the app-layer lane while fixing A47/A48, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: A47's fallback shows restored attachments as ordinary chips and reports through a banner that the models cannot see them. Dismiss the banner and the chips imply the models can see material they cannot - the original defect one step milder: not silently discarded, but silently not loaded. Recorded as a limitation of the fallback the task explicitly allowed, so it is a known bound rather than an unnoticed one.
tasks.fix_summary: The restored-not-loaded state is part of what the chip renders rather than only what a dismissable notice says. `ChatController.attachmentsNotLoaded` exposes the restored documents' ids - derived from the same list `setAttachments`/`addFiles` keep in step, so re-adding a file clears it - `AttachmentBar` passes `isLoaded:`, and `AttachmentChip` shows a warning triangle, the text 'Not loaded - the models cannot see this', an orange fill and border, and a help sentence. A loaded chip is unchanged.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsApp/ChatController.swift and Views/AttachmentBar.swift. swift build --target ChatBots clean; swift test => 815 tests in 136 suites passed. NO TEST: SwiftUI view code in the executable target, unreachable from ChatBotsCoreTests, and the input is the controller's own restore bookkeeping.
tasks.notes: Chosen over adding more banner text because the banner is dismissable BY DESIGN - that is what made it insufficient - whereas the chip is what remains. A warning that can be dismissed is a warning that will be.

tasks.title: The probe's own arguments have the two defects A59 and A62 just fixed in the CLI's
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the CLI lane while fixing A59/A62/A66, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: `--hold` is `Int(value)` with no check and is then gated on `holdSeconds > 0`, so `--hold -5` or `--hold abc` is silently accepted and ignored; and `--port` is `UInt16(value)` with no else branch, so an out-of-range or non-numeric value silently falls back to 7790 - exactly the silent fallback A62 removed from the CLI's `--transport-port`. Both are the 'accepts nonsense silently' class in a run to make the tool report honestly, which is why they are recorded separately rather than folded into A59 or A62.
tasks.fix_summary: `--port` and `--hold` are validated like the rest of the probe's arguments: each names the offending value and exits 2 rather than falling back to a default. `--hold 0` is refused with them, because a hold of nothing is the same false success `--cycles 0` was.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsProbe/main.swift. Run against the built binary: `--port abc`, `--port 0`, `--port 70000`, `--hold abc`, `--hold -1` and `--hold 0` each exit 2 naming the value, and `--cycles 0` still exits 2. The same commands against the pre-fix binary, built from the previous commit in the same .build directory, showed the defect rather than asserting it: `--port abc` printed `cycle 0: FAILED — Could not connect to the conversation engine …` and exited 1 — a connection failure reported for a bad argument — and `--hold -1` did the same while silently not holding. NOT covered by a unit test: the package has no test target for the probe executable, so the evidence is the observed exit codes and messages.
tasks.notes: The pair is the A59/A62 class, and the interesting part is what the old failure looked like: a bad argument was reported as an engine that could not be reached, which sends the reader to the wrong machine. That is the same misattribution A57 recorded (`an unparseable body misreported as 'no model loaded'`) and the reason a usage error has to be a usage error.

tasks.title: Five more CLI flags silently keep their defaults or are silently ignored when they cannot take effect
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the CLI lane while fixing A59/A62/A66, and left unfixed because it falls outside those tasks' scope
tasks.evidence_before: `--turns`, `--max-tokens`, `--compact-threshold`, `--context-window` and `--compact-keep` parse with failable `Int`/`Double` and keep the default when the value is not a number, so `--max-tokens abc` runs with whatever the default was and says nothing. And `--transport` accepts any string but is only consumed under `--serve` (and by `--check-client` through `--transport-port`), so `--transport webtransport` outside those modes is accepted and ignored. This is the A62 and A66 classes, in the same parser, found by the lane that fixed those two and deliberately left unnamed in their entries so the ledger would not be widened after the fact.
tasks.fix_summary: Every flag A114 names is validated at parse time, and `--transport` is refused when `--serve` is absent because no other mode opens a listener. `--backend-a`/`--backend-b` carried the identical defect (`?? .mlx`) and are fixed with them; the accepted backends are listed from `AgentSpec.Backend.allCases` so the message cannot go stale.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCLI/main.swift. Run against the built binary: `--turns abc`, `--turns 0`, `--max-tokens x`, `--context-window 0`, `--compact-keep -3`, `--compact-threshold 5`, `--backend-a nonsense` and `--transport webtransprot --serve` each exit 2 naming the value and what was expected; `--transport http` without `--serve` exits 2; `--help` still exits 0. The same commands against the pre-fix binary, built from the previous commit in the same .build directory, showed the defect: the six silent ones proceeded to run the headless conversation on their defaults, and `--transport webtransprot --serve` printed `ChatBots server listening on http://127.0.0.1:7788` and kept serving — an HTTP-only engine from a typo, which the app cannot connect to. NOT covered by a unit test: the package has no test target for the CLI executable.
tasks.notes: Five of the six were the same two lines of Swift — `if let value = Int(...)` / `Int(...)` with no else — which is why they were recorded as one task: the defect is an idiom, not five independent mistakes. `--compact-keep -3` was the one with teeth: the value reaches `dialogue.dropLast(...)`, which traps on a negative, so the silent default was hiding a crash. The residual worth stating: the flags A114 did not name still use `next() ?? default` for a MISSING value (for example `chatbots-cli --turns` at the end of the line keeps 4). That was outside this task's scope and is not fixed, and it is recorded here rather than left to be rediscovered.

tasks.title: Three MLXEngine methods are synchronous while the protocol requirement is async, so a call on the concrete type silently resolves to the protocol's no-op default
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the A02 lane while wiring a reconfiguration test, and demonstrated with a probe rather than reasoned from the source
tasks.evidence_before: `MLXEngine.setThinking`, `setDisplayName` and `setPersona` are synchronous actor methods, while the `LLMEngine` requirement is `async` and `ChatModels.swift` supplies async no-op defaults in a protocol extension. A call on the CONCRETE `MLXEngine` type therefore resolves to the extension default instead of the real method and does nothing at all. Demonstrated: `await concreteMLXEngine.setThinking(.high)` left `thinking == .off`, while `(engine as any LLMEngine).setThinking(.medium)` set it correctly. It is latent today only because every shipped call site goes through `any LLMEngine` - `ConversationEngine.seatEngine(for:)` returns the existential - so the defect is one type annotation away from being live.
tasks.fix_summary: The three setters on both engines are now `async`, matching the `LLMEngine` requirement by shape as well as by name, so there is no synchronous overload for `await` to lose to and the protocol extension's async no-op is no longer a reachable candidate at a concrete call site. `OpenAIResponsesEngine` carried the identical defect in the same three methods and is fixed with `MLXEngine`. The extension's comment, which claimed the silent default was harmless, now states the hazard instead; the defaults themselves are kept, because a stub or read-only proxy legitimately wants them.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/MLXEngine.swift, OpenAIResponsesEngine.swift, ChatModels.swift:786-802; Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditEngineSetterShadowingTests.swift. The new tests were shown to FAIL before the fix: `await concrete.setThinking(.high)` left `thinking == .off` and `await concrete.setDisplayName("Iris")` left the name at "Mira" on both engines, six failed expectations. After the fix the same tests pass, and a third test pins that the protocol default still compiles, still satisfies the requirement and is still inert for an engine that chooses it. swift test => 818 tests in 137 suites passed, 0 warnings under `.treatAllWarnings(as: .error)`. All shipped call sites already went through `any LLMEngine`, so no call site needed changing.
tasks.notes: This is the A51/A92 class - a control that is presented as working and does nothing - in the one place where the compiler actively helps: an overload that satisfies a protocol by NAME but not by SHAPE is preferred at a concrete call site, and the extension default silently absorbs the call. It was latent only because every call site happened to use the existential, which is the fragile kind of safety: the defect was one type annotation away and no test would have caught it, because every test also used the existential. The generalisation: where a protocol has a silent default, any conformer that declares the member with a different shape gets a split personality, and only a test that names the concrete type can see it.

tasks.title: Dropbox corrupted the build directory: 5 334 conflicted copies inside .build and a module cache compiled at a checkout path that no longer exists
tasks.discovered_by: the coordinator, while verifying the handover's claim that the suite was green - the claim could not be reproduced and the cause was the build directory, not the branch
tasks.evidence_before: `swift test` exited 1 with no test summary at all, failing in the dependency build rather than in this repository's code. Two causes, both environmental. (1) A stale module cache: `precompiled file '.../SwiftShims-2IMTS4WWRU7VJ.pcm' was compiled with module cache path '/Users/andreborchert/Downloads/ChatBots/.build/...', but the path is currently '/Users/andreborchert/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Coding/ChatBots/.build/...'` and `missing required module 'SwiftShims'` - so the build directory had been produced by a checkout at a different path (~/Downloads/ChatBots, which no longer exists). (2) `error: filename "GeneratePlugin.swift" used twice: '.build/checkouts/swift-argument-parser/Plugins/GenerateManual/GenerateCommon (Andre Borchert's conflicted copy 2026-09-13)/GeneratePlugin.swift' and '.../GenerateCommon/GeneratePlugin.swift'`. `find .build -name '*conflicted copy*' | wc -l` => 5334, and `xattr -p com.dropbox.ignored .build` returned nothing, so Dropbox had been syncing build artifacts all along. A109 had marked `.git` ignored after it clobbered the index three times; `.build`, `dist` and `captures` were assumed to be covered because a previous session recorded applying the attribute, and on this disk they were not.
tasks.fix_summary: Removed the corrupted `.build` (5.1 GB) and let SwiftPM rebuild from scratch, and set `com.dropbox.ignored` on `.build`, `dist` and `captures` - verified set this time rather than assumed. The tracked `Package.resolved` is untouched, so the resolved dependency set is unchanged.
tasks.evidence_after: `swift test` on the fresh build directory => exit 0, 'Test run with 815 tests in 136 suites passed'. The failure was never in the branch: the same commit passes with an uncorrupted build directory, which is stated because the alternative reading - that the audit's last wave broke the suite - would have been wrong and alarming.
tasks.notes: Found by trying to REPRODUCE a number before documenting it, which is the habit this whole audit has been built on: the handover was about to assert a green suite on the strength of a lane's report, and checking it found a 5 GB corrupted directory instead. The pattern across A109 and A116 is one omission with two consequences - Dropbox was allowed to sync things it should not, git internals in one case and build artifacts in the other - and in both cases the attribute was believed rather than checked. The generalisation worth carrying into the next session: on this machine, every directory that is regenerable (`.build`, `dist`, `captures`, and `.git`) must be verified as Dropbox-ignored, because Dropbox mutates what it syncs and a build directory full of conflicted copies fails in ways that look like source defects.

tasks.title: The done-commit guard separated its fields with U+0001, which bash consumes as its own CTLESC marker, so it skipped all 109 DONE tasks and exited 0
tasks.discovered_by: the incoming session, while verifying the handover's claim that the guard exits 0 with 97 tasks backed — the claim did not reproduce on the verification host
tasks.evidence_before: `AUDIT/verify-done-commits.sh` exited 0 reporting `backed 0 · skipped 109 · unbacked 0`. Every DONE task was skipped as 'names no source path', including A29 (which names `APIServer.swift` and `EngineService.swift`) and A30 (`HTTPServer.swift:184,191`), so the skip was not a property of those tasks. The rows were correct — `jq ... | join("\u0001")` emits U+0001, confirmed with `xxd` — but `while IFS=$'\001' read -r id commit file_line unit` never split them: `$id` held the entire row. Reproduced in isolation on macOS bash 3.2.57: `IFS=$'\001'` over `a\001b\001c` yields `[abc][][]`, while IFS `:`, tab, U+0002, U+001C, U+001E and U+001F all split correctly. U+0001 is bash's internal CTLESC escape character — U+007F is CTLNUL — so a literal one cannot survive in a shell variable: the delimiter was consumed by the shell that was meant to read it. This is A83 exactly inverted, that guard skipped the tasks it existed to catch and this one skipped every task, and it was invisible for the same reason: a skip is reported rather than failed, and the exit status was 0 either way. The consequence is that Phase C's rule ('verify-done-commits.sh must exit 0 before a fix task is called DONE') was being satisfied by checking nothing, and Phase E section 10/12, which passes on this exit status, would have printed the vacuous count as a pass.
tasks.fix_summary: The separator is now U+001F, which is not IFS whitespace (so an empty field stays an empty field, the property A83 needed) and is not one of bash's internal markers. The parse is also checked rather than trusted, so the failure cannot be silent again: a row whose first field is not a task id aborts with exit 2, and the number of rows read must equal the number of DONE tasks in the ledger. The header records both failures and why the third delimiter is different, because the file had already been wrong twice in the same direction.
tasks.evidence_after: `bash AUDIT/verify-done-commits.sh` on macOS bash 3.2.57, the shell the verification host ships: `backed 97 · skipped 12 · unbacked 0`, exit 0 — the figure the handover claimed. The 12 skipped name no `.swift`/`.py`/`.sh` path by design (A01, A06, A11, A12, A13, A28, A79, A84, A87, A98, A109, A116). Four mutations of `AUDIT/ledger.json`, each required to fail and each does: a DONE task with an empty `commit` -> `FAIL A29 ... commit is 'empty'`, exit 1; a commit that touches none of the named paths (`a3156ce` for A29) -> `FAIL A29 ... touches none of`, exit 1; a commit that is not in the repository (`deadbeef`) -> `FAIL A29 ... not in this repository`, exit 1; a row whose id is not a task id -> `FATAL`, exit 2.
tasks.notes: Found the same way A116 was found, and by the handover's own rule: the claim did not reproduce, and the cause was the mechanism rather than the work. The fix has the same shape as A116's — make the mechanism fail loudly on the input it was silently tolerating. A residual is recorded rather than claimed away: this guard proves a DONE task's commit touches a path the task names, not that the change is correct or complete; and a task naming only a bare basename can be satisfied by any file with that name, which is why a full path is preferred wherever the ledger gives one.

tasks.file_line: AUDIT/ledger.md:16-31 (the Summary and Open tasks tables), AUDIT/render-ledger.sh
