tasks.discovered_by: the incoming session, while locating the ledger to record a new finding
tasks.evidence_before: `AUDIT/HANDOVER.md:4` says 'ledger.md is still the source of truth and wins on any conflict with this page', `:19` repeats it, and `:109` instructs the next session to 'Read AUDIT/ledger.md first'. `AUDIT/plan.md:119` states the same. The file does not match that claim: its Summary asserts 'Tasks enumerated | 28' and 'DONE | 9', its `## Open tasks` table lists only A01-A05, and `grep -cE '^#+ A[0-9]+'` finds 26 task headings against 116 tasks in `ledger.json`. `grep -c` for each of A90, A95, A100, A105, A110, A113, A114, A115 and A116 in ledger.md returns 0. A reader following the handover would conclude the audit enumerated 28 tasks and closed 9.
tasks.fix_summary: The status content of ledger.md is generated from ledger.json by AUDIT/render-ledger.sh, which rewrites only the region between two markers and leaves every prose section untouched; `--check` renders and diffs, failing on drift. The page now states which artifact is authoritative - ledger.json, the thing every gate reads - and the same wrong claim was corrected in HANDOVER.md (:3-5, :19, :113) and plan.md (:119). The renderer parses before it writes and refuses to emit anything if the ledger will not parse, rather than rendering an empty status that would read as a ledger with no tasks, which is A89 applied to the tool that records A89.
tasks.evidence_after: AUDIT/render-ledger.sh, AUDIT/ledger.md, AUDIT/phase-e.sh section 12, .github/workflows/checks.yml generated-files job. `bash AUDIT/render-ledger.sh --check` exits 0 when in step and 1 on drift; proved by mutating A77 to DONE in ledger.json, observing exit 1 with the rendered diff, and restoring the file so that `cmp` against the backup is identical. The region now enumerates all 122 tasks, where the hand-written tables named 28 and stopped at A89. Phase E section 12 and the CI job both fail on drift, and the shell-parse step now covers AUDIT/*.sh as well as tools/*.sh.
tasks.notes: The third instance in this audit of one pattern: a document asserting a state the artifact does not have (A111, A112, and the six findings whose tests encoded their own defect). It is also the same remedy the repository already applies to web/ and names/ - stop hand-maintaining a summary of generated facts, and make drift a failing gate - so the fix reuses a convention a reader already knows rather than inventing one. A residual is stated rather than hidden: this makes the status tables true, it does not make the prose a substitute for ledger.json, and the prose sections for A01-A89 remain the earlier wave's writing.

tasks.title: The page POSTs a layout diagnostic to /api/client-report, a route that has never existed in any commit, and the 404 is swallowed by design
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the client-layer pass, and confirmed against the whole history before it was recorded
tasks.evidence_before: `web/app.js:1393` posts `{width, height, pixelRatio, device, layout, scrollWidth, profile, overflowing}` to `/api/client-report`, inside a `try` whose `catch` is explicitly empty ('a diagnostic that fails must not break the page', `:1401`). `grep -rn 'client-report'` over the repository finds only the two generated copies of the page — `web/app.js` and `WebAssets.swift` — and no route, and `APIServer.translate`'s `default:` returns nil for it. `git log -S 'client-report' --all -- Sources/ChatBotsCore/APIServer.swift` returns nothing, so the string has never been in the server in any commit: the receiving end was never written, rather than removed. `ClientReport` (`APIServer.swift:231`, documented as 'What the client measured about its own layout', carrying `overflowing`: 'Selectors of elements wider than the viewport, worst first') is referenced nowhere else in `Sources/` or `Tests/`. So the page measures the layout on every load, posts it to nothing, and the failure is deliberately invisible.
tasks.fix_summary: The diagnostic reports to the browser console instead of POSTing to a route that does not exist, and the unused `ClientReport` payload type is removed from the server. The measurement itself is unchanged: it still names the elements wider than the viewport, worst first, because that is what answers the question the flag is for.
tasks.evidence_after: web/app.js (reportLayout and its call site), Sources/ChatBotsCore/WebAssets.swift (regenerated), Sources/ChatBotsCore/APIServer.swift (the ClientReport declaration removed). `grep -n 'api.post("/api/client-report"' web/app.js` finds nothing; `grep -rn 'ClientReport'` over Sources/ and Tests/ finds nothing. `node --check web/app.js` parses. `python3 tools/embed-web.py --check` reports the embedded asset in step, and EmbeddedWebAssetTests enforces the same byte-for-byte invariant, so Caddy and the engine serve the same page. `swift test` => 821 tests in 138 suites passed. NOT verified in a browser: the console output itself, which needs the page loaded with ?diag=1; the code path is a straight-line replacement of a request with two console calls, and the page's parsing and embedding are both gated.
tasks.notes: The tempting fix was to implement the route, and it was rejected: it would add an unauthenticated write endpoint reachable from the LAN (A01) to serve a developer-only flag, which is exactly the surface A75 and A76 closed, and nothing consumes the report except a human reading a log. Removing a control that cannot work is the precedent A51 (a Models menu that loaded nothing) and A64 (dead pool API) set. This is also the third finding from the same shape - a client and a contract that were never joined up - after A62's silently-swallowed transport port and A120's unused HTTP port, and it is the reason both of those were found by running the built artifact rather than by reading it.

tasks.title: The engine the app spawns opens an HTTP listener on 7788 that the app does not use, so it cannot start at all while Caddy holds that port
tasks.discovered_by: the incoming session, following the port question raised by the client-layer pass
tasks.evidence_before: `EngineSupervisor.launch` starts the engine with `--serve --transport webtransport --transport-port 7790` and no `--port`, and its own comment says the app 'does not use the engine's HTTP server, and asking for it was actively harmful'. But `--serve` constructs `APIServer(port: options.port)` and calls `server.start()` unconditionally (`main.swift:754-758`), before the transport branch at `:781`, and `options.port` defaults to 7788 (`:50`). A bind failure is fatal to the child: `:761-770` writes 'could not start the server on port ...' or 'the port is already in use' and exits. The documented website deployment publishes exactly that port — `Caddyfile:27` is `http://:7788`, on all interfaces, started by `tools/start.sh` — so in the configuration the README documents, opening the desktop app while Caddy is running and nothing is answering on 7790 makes the spawned engine exit on a port collision that has nothing to do with the transport, and the app reports an engine that failed to start. That this collision is real is shown by the code's own workaround elsewhere: `TransportCheck` passes `--port String(port - 1)` with the comment 'A port that is not in use, so the HTTP listener cannot collide with a real run' (`TransportCheck.swift:139-140`).
tasks.fix_summary: `--serve` opens its HTTP listener only when the requested transport includes HTTP. The `APIServer` is still always built, because it owns the one `EngineService` both transports dispatch through — only the listener is conditional. The engine the app's supervisor spawns asks for `--transport webtransport`, so it now binds no HTTP port at all and the collision with the port Caddy publishes is gone. `--transport http` and `--transport both` are unchanged. A comment in `TransportCheck` that justified passing an unused `--port` by that same collision was corrected, since the collision it described can no longer happen in that mode.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCLI/main.swift (the serve block). Before and after were measured on the built binary with 127.0.0.1:7788 held by a python http.server standing in for Caddy: BEFORE `chatbots-cli --serve --transport webtransport --transport-port 7799 --port 7788` printed `could not start the server on port 7788: Port 7788 is already in use` and exited 1; AFTER the same command printed `http : not served (--transport webtransport)`, `app : webtransport://127.0.0.1:7799` and served until SIGTERM, which it handled cleanly with exit 0. Regressions checked the same way: `--transport http --port 7797` logs the HTTP routes and serves, and `--transport both --port 7797 --transport-port 7798` serves HTTP and logs the WebTransport endpoint. NOT covered by a unit test: the package has no test target for the CLI executable, so this is an observed runtime difference; the suite run after the change aborted inside Network.framework, which is A102's recorded flake reproduced rather than anything this change introduced (the change is in the CLI target, which the test suite does not compile).
tasks.notes: The finding is one of the class where the code disagreed with its own comment: `EngineSupervisor` says the app 'does not use the engine's HTTP server, and asking for it was actively harmful', and then asked for it with a bare `--serve`. The fix makes the code match the comment rather than the comment match the code. The `APIServer`-owns-the-`EngineService` detail is why the obvious fix (do not construct it) is wrong, and it is the reason this is a gating change rather than a removal.

tasks.title: The installer accepts macOS 14 while the package and the bundle require macOS 26, so a Sonoma user downloads ~3 GB and builds before the app refuses to launch
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the tooling pass as an inconsistency between install.sh and Package.swift, verified line by line before recording
tasks.evidence_before: `tools/install.sh:99-100` gates on `[ "$OS_MAJOR" -lt 14 ]` and dies with 'macOS 14 (Sonoma) or newer is required', so it proceeds on macOS 14 and 15. `Package.swift:38` requires `.macOS(.v26)`, `tools/make-app.sh` writes `<key>LSMinimumSystemVersion</key><string>26.0</string>`, and `README.md:96` states 'macOS 26 or newer'. On macOS 14 or 15 the installer therefore downloads the checkpoint (~3 GB per its own text at :65 and :216), installs a toolchain if none is present, and builds the app — and the app then cannot launch, because the bundle declares a minimum system version the host does not meet. The project already treats this pair of declarations as one fact: `checks.yml:42-51` fails the push when `make-app.sh`'s `LSMinimumSystemVersion` and `Package.swift`'s `.macOS(.v…)` disagree, but nothing checks the installer against either, so the third declaration was free to drift and did. Its disk-space text is stale in the same place: `:79` says 'the models alone are ~6 GB' while the installer downloads one ~3 GB checkpoint.
tasks.fix_summary: The installer no longer declares a minimum macOS. It reads it from `Package.swift`, which is the value the app bundle copies and that CI already checks the bundle against, so the duplicate that drifted from 14 to 26 three major versions late is gone rather than policed. The disk-space message now describes the ~3 GB download it actually performs instead of claiming ~6 GB of models.
tasks.evidence_after: tools/install.sh:97-111, .github/workflows/checks.yml (generated-files job). `bash -n tools/install.sh` parses. The extraction `grep -oE '\.macOS\(\.v[0-9]+\)' Package.swift | grep -oE '[0-9]+' | head -1` returns 26, and the gate was simulated on this host: 26 >= 26 proceeds, 14 < 26 refuses. The new CI step was run against the fixed file, where it exits 0, and its pattern was exercised against three inputs: the old `[ "$OS_MAJOR" -lt 14 ]` matches, a reintroduced `[ "$OS_MAJOR" -lt 26 ]` matches, and the unrelated `[ "$attempt" -lt 3 ]` does not. NOT verifiable here: the macOS 14 refusal itself, since this host runs 26 and no Sonoma machine is in the fleet.
tasks.notes: The change is a deletion of a duplicated fact rather than a new check, which is the same judgement A118 made about the ledger's status tables: where two artifacts had to agree and one was unguarded, remove the unguarded value instead of adding a third thing to keep in step. The first version of the CI guard was wrong in the way this audit keeps finding - it matched `-lt 3` in the retry loop, so it would have failed the build for a defect that was not there - and that is recorded because a guard that fires on the wrong input is as bad as one that skips the right one.

tasks.title: TransportCheck declares a timeout it never uses and creates both child pipes without ever draining them
tasks.discovered_by: reported by the client-layer pass, verified by reading the whole file
tasks.evidence_before: `TransportCheck.run(in:port:timeout:)` declares `timeout: Duration = .seconds(30)` (`:100`) and `grep -n timeout` over the file finds that line and nothing else, so the parameter is dead: the check that the installer's smoke test runs has no overall deadline of its own. The same function sets `engineProcess.standardOutput = Pipe()` and `standardError = Pipe()` (`:142-143`) and never reads either — no `readabilityHandler`, no `availableData`, no drain — so the child's log output accumulates in a pipe buffer, and a child that writes more than the buffer holds blocks on the write and is waited on forever. Both are shapes this audit has already recorded elsewhere: a timeout that cannot fire is A36, a control presented as working that does nothing is A51, and a child that can block on an undrained pipe is the same family as A36's blocking drain. In practice `install.sh` wraps the invocation in a portable 180-second timeout, so the installer is bounded from outside; the check itself is not, and `chatbots-cli --check-transport` run directly is unbounded.
tasks.fix_summary: `timeout` now sets the client's request budget and bounds the connect retry loop by one wall-clock deadline; the child's stdout and stderr go to the null device instead of to pipes no one reads. The budget mapping is extracted as a pure function so the part that needs no socket is testable.
tasks.evidence_after: Sources/ChatBotsCore/TransportCheck.swift; Tests/ChatBotsCoreTests/AuditTransportCheckTimeoutTests.swift. Three tests: the budget mapping (30s -> 30000ms, 1s -> 1000ms, 250ms -> 250ms), the floor (a zero, sub-millisecond or negative budget becomes 1ms rather than a deadline that has already passed), and the clamp (a budget too large for `Int32` returns `Int32.max` instead of trapping, which the first implementation of this helper did). swift test => 821 tests in 138 suites passed, 0 warnings. NOT verifiable in the suite: the spawned child and the pipe behaviour need a real engine process, so the drain is argued from the code and the check's own report rather than measured.
tasks.notes: The pipes are the A36 shape recorded a second time: a resource created and never consumed, where the failure is a hang rather than a wrong answer. Recorded as an observation rather than folded into this task: the same function also builds a `ConversationEngine` on line 121 and discards it (`_ = engine`), with a comment claiming it is what makes the check about the channel rather than about weights — but the check spawns a separate process and never uses that engine, so both the engine and `TransportCheckEngine` are dead weight. That is a separate finding and is not fixed here.

tasks.title: The build gate counted SwiftPM's dependency-cache notices as compiler warnings, so a clean tree failed the acceptance run
tasks.discovered_by: the first Phase E run, from a fresh clone on node1
tasks.evidence_before: Phase E failed `3/12 build` with `build produced 4 warning line(s) despite warnings-as-errors`. The four lines were one per dependency, all of the same shape: `warning: 'swift-jinja': skipping cache due to an error: The file "maintenance.lock" doesn't exist.` SwiftPM prints these about its own package cache. They are not statements about this repository's code, and they are not governed by `treatAllWarnings(as: .error)` — which is set in `Package.swift`, so a compiler warning cannot survive the build at all. The gate's grep for `warning:` therefore measured SwiftPM's chatter rather than the thing the setting controls, and a green tree failed for a reason that has nothing to do with the tree.
tasks.fix_summary: The gate counts compiler diagnostics by shape — lines matching `.swift:<line>:<col>: warning:` — and reports SwiftPM's notices separately in the pass line, so they are visible without being mistaken for findings. The check still guards the setting rather than duplicating it: a build that succeeds has no compiler warnings by construction, so the line exists to catch someone removing the setting.
tasks.evidence_after: AUDIT/phase-e.sh section 3. On the fresh clone the gate now reports the compiler-warning count it is about and names the number of SwiftPM notices it did not count. Verified by the second Phase E run: section 3 passes.
tasks.notes: The gate was written when the tree had just been made warning-free, and it assumed the string `warning:` belonged to the compiler. This is A28's lesson again in a different instrument — the count was taken from a broad textual match rather than from the thing being counted — and the fix is the same shape: read the figure from the object that owns it.

tasks.title: The dependency gate scanned the sanitizer scratch directories and reported 16 vulnerabilities from third-party example projects, not from this repository's resolved set
tasks.discovered_by: the first Phase E run, while reading the report it wrote
tasks.evidence_before: Phase E failed `8/12 dependency vulnerabilities` with `Total 8 packages affected by 16 known vulnerabilities (0 Critical, 8 High, 8 Medium)`. The report's own log says what it walked: `Scanned .../scratch-tsan/checkouts/swift-transformers/Examples/Mistral7B/requirements.txt`, `.../mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx-c/docs/requirements.txt`, `.../swift-huggingface/Package.resolved`, and so on. Those directories are the ASan and TSan scratch build trees, each holding every dependency's own checkout — including its example projects and their Python requirements — so the scan was reading code this repository does not ship and never declares. The baseline's `no issues found` was recorded before those directories existed, which is why the drift went unnoticed.
tasks.fix_summary: Scoped to the object the gate is about: `osv-scanner scan source --lockfile Package.resolved`, the same resolved set the lockfile gate and the third-party notices are about, instead of `-r .`.
tasks.evidence_after: AUDIT/phase-e.sh section 8. `osv-scanner scan source --lockfile Package.resolved` on the same tree reports `Scanned .../Package.resolved file and found 14 packages` and `No issues found` — 14 packages, matching `Package.resolved`, rather than 8 ecosystems' worth of other people's examples. Verified by the second Phase E run: section 8 passes.
tasks.notes: The gate passed at baseline because the scratch directories did not exist yet, which is the general hazard of a recursive scan in a gate: it measures whatever happens to be on disk at the time, and its own evidence directories count. Scoping it to the lockfile also makes it agree with `tools/third-party-notices.py`, which checks the same 14 packages — two gates about one object should name that object.

tasks.title: The style gates measured generated code and the recorded waivers were below the tree they govern, so Phase E could not have passed on the branch it was written for
tasks.discovered_by: the first Phase E run, and then by measuring the handover head's own counts rather than assuming the recorded ones were current
tasks.evidence_before: Two problems, and the second was not visible from the first. (1) `swift-format lint --recursive Sources Tests` lints the generated `Sources/ChatBotsCore/WebAssets.swift`, which embeds `web/` at column 0: 2 253 of the recorded 3 003 diagnostics were indentation findings in that one generated file, out of ~2 300 in generated files in total. The count was therefore a function of the web interface, and editing a line of `web/app.js` moved the waiver by 17 — measured. `swiftlint` already excluded both generated files (`.swiftlint.yml`, A06); `swift-format` did not. (2) Running the same gates over the handover head `9eafa54` gives `swiftlint` **256** and authored-only `swift-format` **744**, against recorded waivers of **222** and **3 003**. So the `swiftlint` waiver was already 34 below the tree it governs — later audit waves added findings without re-measuring — and the branch's own Phase E could not have passed. The audit's own changes had added 11 findings: three `OrderedImports` in new test files, two `optional_data_string_conversion` in a test I added, and six over-long messages in the CLI.
tasks.fix_summary: Both style gates now lint authored Swift only — the same two generated files `.swiftlint.yml` already excluded, applied to `swift-format` in `AUDIT/phase-e.sh` and `tools/audit-checks.sh` through an explicit file list, because `swift-format` has no exclude option. The 11 findings this session added are fixed rather than waived: the import order and the two conversions in the tests, and the six long CLI messages, which are now one `reject()` helper instead of ten copies of the same sentence (that refactor removed nine findings net, including two of A62's). Both waivers are re-recorded in `plan.md` with the method that produced them and why each previous number was wrong.
tasks.evidence_after: `swiftlint` **255** and authored `swift-format` **744**, in `AUDIT/plan.md`. The authored-only `swift-format` count is **744 at the handover head and 744 now**, so this session added none; the `swiftlint` count fell from 256 to 255. The CLI's messages were re-run after the refactor and are unchanged: `--turns abc`, `--transport typo --serve`, `--backend-a nonsense`, `--share-base notaurl`, `--compact-keep -3`, `--port 0` and `--transport-port 99999` each still exit 2 with the same wording. Verified by the second Phase E run, sections 9 and 12.
tasks.notes: This is the fifth defect the audit has found in its own measurement rather than in the product, and the same lesson each time: **a count is only as good as the object it is taken from.** A28 found three figures that were the line counts of captured files; A83 and A117 found guards that skipped their own targets; A123 and A124 found gates reading SwiftPM's chatter and other people's example projects; this one found a waiver quoted from a state the tree had left behind. The generalisation now written into `plan.md`: the waiver is the measured residual, not a budget, and a change that raises it has to edit the line and say why.

tasks.title: A99's layout diagnostic passed a template literal to console.info, which semgrep reports as an unsafe format string
tasks.discovered_by: the first Phase E run's semgrep gate, as the one finding not covered by a waiver
tasks.evidence_before: Phase E section 9 failed with `UNWAIVED: javascript.lang.security.audit.unsafe-formatstring.unsafe-formatstring web/app.js`. The site was the line A99 introduced when the diagnostic moved from the dead `/api/client-report` POST to the console: `console.info(\`${overflowing.length} element(s) wider than the viewport, worst first:\`, overflowing.slice(0, 6))`. A non-literal first argument to a console call is how a format specifier in the data would be interpreted as one; here the data is a number this script computed, so it was not exploitable, but it is exactly the pattern the rule exists to stop and it was new in this session.
tasks.fix_summary: The message is a literal and the variable parts are arguments: `console.info("elements wider than the viewport, worst first:", overflowing.length, overflowing.slice(0, 6))`. No interpolation, same output for the developer reading the console.
tasks.evidence_after: `semgrep --config auto --json web/app.js | jq '.results | length'` returns 0; the page is regenerated into `WebAssets.swift` and `tools/embed-web.py --check` is in step; `node --check web/app.js` parses; the full suite is green. Verified by the second Phase E run: section 9's semgrep gate passes with only the three written waivers.
tasks.notes: Found by the audit's own gate on code the audit had just written, which is the control working in the direction people forget: the gates are not only for the code that was there before. It is also the first finding this session that a linter caught rather than a reader.

tasks.title: The acceptance statement reported the done-commit gate as passing with an empty count, because it read the blank line above the summary
tasks.discovered_by: the first Phase E run, reading its own summary rather than its exit status
tasks.evidence_before: The summary line read `PASS|verify-done-commits.sh: ` with nothing after the colon. Section 10 takes `tail -2 "$out/done-commits.txt" | head -1`, and the guard ends with a blank line before its `backed N · skipped M · unbacked K` summary, so the two-line form selected the blank. A gate that passes while printing no figure is one a reader cannot check, and this is the gate the whole audit rests on — 'verify-done-commits.sh must exit 0 before a fix task is called DONE'. A117 changed that guard's output while fixing its delimiter and did not notice this reader.
tasks.fix_summary: `tail -1`, so the acceptance statement prints the count it is asserting.
tasks.evidence_after: The second Phase E run's summary reads `PASS|verify-done-commits.sh: backed 110 · skipped 12 · unbacked 0`.
tasks.notes: The same class as A117 itself: the guard was right and the thing reading it was not. It was found by reading the summary rather than the exit status, which is the habit that found A116 and A102 as well.

tasks.title: The build gate's error count matched SwiftPM's cache notices, so a green section reported four errors
tasks.discovered_by: reading the second Phase E run's own summary rather than its exit status — the run passed, and one line in it was false
tasks.evidence_before: The green acceptance run printed `PASS|swift build --build-tests: 4 errors, 0 compiler warnings (4 SwiftPM notice(s) not counted)`. The build had exited 0 and the suite had run, so there were no errors: the four were SwiftPM's dependency-cache notices, whose text is `skipping cache due to an error: The file "maintenance.lock" doesn't exist`, and the expression was `grep -cE 'error:'`. A123 fixed the warning count on that same line and left the error count beside it, with the same defect — the second time the audit has read a count from a broad textual match instead of from the object that owns it.
tasks.fix_summary: Both counts on that line are taken by diagnostic shape, `.swift:<line>:<col>: error:` and `: warning:`, and the SwiftPM notices are reported once as a number so they cannot be mistaken for either.
tasks.evidence_after: `grep -cE '\.swift:[0-9]+:[0-9]+: error:'` over the build log from the failing run returns 0, so the line now reads `0 compiler errors`. `bash -n AUDIT/phase-e.sh` parses. Verified by the third Phase E run: section 3 passes and reports zero of both.
tasks.notes: Recorded as its own task rather than folded into A123, because A123's fix was committed and pushed before this was seen: the audit's rule is that a finding gets an id the moment it is found, and 'the fix for A123 was incomplete' is a finding about A123's fix. The wider point is the same one A28, A123, A124 and A125 make: a gate that greps for a word measures every line containing the word, so the count has to be taken from the diagnostic the tool emits.

tasks.title: The CI semgrep step ran with `--error` and would have failed on the very findings the audit waived in writing, and it had never executed because the workflow does not run on the audit branch
tasks.discovered_by: the session that landed the audit, by asking whether the CI it was about to enable had ever run — it had not
tasks.evidence_before: The `static-analysis` job's last step was `semgrep scan --config auto --error Sources tools web`. A09 waived three findings in `tools/cdp.py` in writing, in `AUDIT/plan.md`, and deliberately did not suppress them — there is no `nosemgrep`, because that hides a finding rather than justifying it — so `--error` fails on exactly those three. Reproduced on a clean export of the tree (`git archive`, no `.build`, no scratch): `Ran 461 rules on 87 files: 3 findings`, exit 1. The gate had never run: the workflow triggers on `push: branches: [main]` and `pull_request`, and all of this work is on `audit/2026-09-13`, so the job would have failed the first time it executed — on `main`, after the landing, which is the worst moment to find it. The Mac-side gate in `phase-e.sh` had the correct logic (an allowlist matched on rule id and path suffix), so the two gates also disagreed about what had been justified.
tasks.fix_summary: The allowlist is now one implementation, `tools/semgrep-waivers.py`, called by both the CI job and `AUDIT/phase-e.sh`, so the hosted gate and the Mac gate cannot disagree. Semgrep runs without `--error` and writes JSON; the script matches each finding against the `semgrep waiver: <rule> <path>` lines in `AUDIT/plan.md` and fails only on a finding that no waiver covers. It exits 2 rather than 0 when the report is missing or unparseable, because a report that cannot be read is not a clean one (A89).
tasks.evidence_after: tools/semgrep-waivers.py, .github/workflows/checks.yml, AUDIT/phase-e.sh. Four cases exercised: the real report gives `semgrep: 3 finding(s), all covered by a recorded waiver`, exit 0; a fourth, unwaived finding added to it gives exit 1 naming the rule and path; an unparseable report gives exit 2; a missing report gives exit 2. The exact CI steps were then run on a clean export of the tree: semgrep exit 0, waiver check exit 0, shellcheck/ruff/pyright/gitleaks/osv all exit 0.
tasks.notes: This is the fourth time this audit has found a control that had never been exercised — after A89 (a gate that passed on a ledger it could not parse), A102 (a test suite that aborted under a concurrency the suite itself created) and A123-A127 (five gates the first Phase E run had never reached in that combination). The generalisable question, now asked before landing: **has this check ever actually run in the place it will run?** A gate that is only written is not a gate.

tasks.title: The CI dependency step scanned the whole tree with `-r .` — the same defect A124 fixed in phase-e.sh, in the second copy of the same check
tasks.discovered_by: the same question that found A129: what has never run, and what would it do if it did?
tasks.evidence_before: The step was `osv-scanner scan source -r .`, where `phase-e.sh` had already been corrected to `--lockfile Package.resolved` for A124. On a clean CI checkout the recursive form happens to be harmless — measured: it finds only `Package.resolved` and reports `No issues found` — because there are no dependency checkouts in the tree. That is luck rather than correctness: the same command in the Mac gate reported 16 vulnerabilities from dependencies' own example projects inside the sanitizer scratch directories, and `AUDIT/baseline/` already contains captured scanner output that a future recursive scan could read.
tasks.fix_summary: Scoped to `--lockfile Package.resolved`, the object the check is about and the same object `tools/third-party-notices.py` checks.
tasks.evidence_after: `.github/workflows/checks.yml`; `osv-scanner scan source --lockfile Package.resolved` on a clean export reports 14 packages and no issues. Both gates now name the same object.
tasks.notes: Recorded separately from A124 rather than folded in, because it is a different file and a different copy of the defect — and because A124's fix would have been described as complete while a second instance remained. It is the same lesson as A129: a fix applied where the problem was found, rather than everywhere it exists, leaves the next surface wrong.

tasks.title: The CI install step verified its own installs before GITHUB_PATH applied, so the job died with exit 127 on its first real run
tasks.discovered_by: the first push to main, from the CI run the landing triggered — the same question as A129 and A130, one level further down
tasks.evidence_before: The `static-analysis` job failed in its *install* step, not in any gate: `ShellCheck - shell script analysis tool / version: 0.9.0` — the runner image's version, not the pinned 0.11.0 — then `line 25: gitleaks: command not found`, `##[error]Process completed with exit code 127`. `GITHUB_PATH` takes effect for the next step, not the one that writes it, so the version lines at the bottom of the step resolved against the image: they found the image's shellcheck and could not find `gitleaks` at all, though the step had downloaded it a few lines earlier into a directory not yet on `PATH`. Every download, the venv and the npm install had succeeded; the step failed while proving its own work. GitHub run `checks` #11 on `5398362`, job `Lint, type-check and scan`, step 3.
tasks.fix_summary: `export PATH="$tools/bin:$tools/venv/bin:$PATH"` beside the `GITHUB_PATH` lines, so the step uses the tools it just installed. That is also what those lines are for: they are meant to prove the pinned version is the one that runs, and against the image they proved nothing.
tasks.evidence_after: `.github/workflows/checks.yml`; rehearsed locally against the same shell semantics (with the export the pinned script resolves). Verified on GitHub: `checks` #12 on `8c4174f` — **completed success**, with the install step and all seven analysis steps green — and `checks` #13 on `73eac3b` after the next landing, also success.
tasks.notes: The third defect found by asking one question: **has this ever actually run?** A129 and A130 were in the gates, this one was in the machinery that installs them, and it could only fail on the first execution — which is exactly what a workflow that does not trigger on the development branch guarantees. The generalisation recorded with A129 stands, and this is its sharpest instance: the failure was in the step whose entire job is to make the others trustworthy.

tasks.title: The acceptance script refused to run on main, the branch the audit had just been landed on
tasks.discovered_by: the first acceptance run made after the landing
tasks.evidence_before: Phase E on `main` at `5398362` reported 22 passed, 1 failed, and the one failure was the script's own identity check: `FAIL|on branch 'main', not audit/2026-09-13`. Everything the run measures passed — 824 tests in 139 suites, both sanitizers clean, coverage 77.03 %, gitleaks 0 over the full history, osv clean, semgrep's three findings all waived, shellcheck/ruff/pyright clean, swiftlint 255 and authored swift-format 744 at their waivers, the guard at backed 116 · skipped 14 · unbacked 0, and 130 tasks with none open. The check's intent was "not on some arbitrary branch", and after the landing `main` is the branch that matters — a gate that refuses to run where the code ships is a gate that stops being run.
tasks.fix_summary: The check accepts `audit/2026-09-13` or `main` and says which it found; any other branch still fails. The §0 comment beside it now explains why the `origin/main` figure it records means something different either side of the landing — before, it is the branch's distance from the base commit; after, it is the whole history.
tasks.evidence_after: AUDIT/phase-e.sh. The acceptance run on `main` at `73eac3bd` then reported **23 passed, 0 failed**, with `PASS|on main, which the audit was landed on` — `AUDIT/baseline/phaseE/summary.txt`. `bash -n AUDIT/phase-e.sh` parses.
tasks.notes: A small thing with a pointed lesson: the audit's own instruments encoded the *circumstances* of the audit — which branch it ran on — rather than its invariant, which is that the run describes a commit. `90e9f7b6` was accepted on the audit branch and `73eac3bd` is accepted on `main`; both are the same tree, and the identity file in each run names the commit rather than the branch label.

tasks.title: Xcode 27 ships the Metal compiler as a separate downloadable component and nothing in the repository requires or checks it, so a clean Xcode 27 machine cannot build the package at all
tasks.discovered_by: Phase A baseline build under Swift 6.4
tasks.evidence_before: `swift build --build-tests` on a clean `.build` under Xcode 27.0 / Swift 6.4 failed: `error: CompileMetalFile .../mlx-swift/.../steel/attn/kernels/steel_attention.metal failed with a nonzero exit code` + `error: Build failed` (exit 1). The real diagnostic is only visible by running the compiler by hand: `xcrun -sdk macosx metal --version` -> `error: cannot execute tool 'metal' due to missing Metal Toolchain; use: xcodebuild -downloadComponent MetalToolchain`. Xcode 27 no longer bundles the Metal compiler. `tools/install.sh` checks for Swift, `iconutil`/`sips`/`plutil`/`textutil` and the macOS version but never for Metal; `README.md` Requirements says only Apple silicon + macOS 26 + disk/memory. Measured by execution on all four Macs: node1 works (after this audit installed it), node2/node3/node4 fail. `xcrun --find metal` returns a path even where the component is absent, so a path-only check reports false success.
tasks.fix_summary: New `tools/check-metal.sh` executes `xcrun -sdk macosx metal --version` and, on failure, prints the compiler diagnostic, the missing component and the install command; `tools/install.sh` calls it before the model download and stops there; `README.md` documents the component and that `xcrun --find metal` cannot detect its absence. The component was installed on node2, the Phase E host.
tasks.evidence_after: Measured on real hosts (`AUDIT/baseline/swift64/a133-metal.log`). `tools/check-metal.sh` passes on node1 (`Apple metal version 32023.921`) and on node2, which was given the component for Phase E during this task; node2 was then verified by *compiling* a real kernel, not by reading a version string — `xcrun -sdk macosx metal -c metal-smoke.metal` exits 0 and writes a 3 296-byte `.air`. On node3 it exits 1 with the diagnostic, the missing component and `xcodebuild -downloadComponent MetalToolchain`, while `xcrun --find metal` on the same host prints `/Applications/Xcode.app/.../metal` and exits 0 — the false success the finding is about, reproduced on a machine that has not been fixed. `tools/install.sh` was then run with a stub `xcrun` that fails: it stops at the Metal step, exits 1 and never reaches the model download (the log is in the commit). `shellcheck` is clean on both scripts; `README.md` carries the command and the caveat.
tasks.notes: The install itself is not a repository change, so the evidence for it is the fleet output in `AUDIT/baseline/swift64/a133-metal.log` and the updated rows in `environment.md`. One thing worth recording because it looks alarming and is not: `xcodebuild -runFirstLaunch` on node2 printed `Install Failed: Authorization is required to install the packages`, which is the system-wide install step wanting an administrator. The toolchain is nevertheless usable — the asset is mounted on demand through the cryptex, which is why `--find` returned a `/var/run/com.apple.security.cryptexd/...` path afterwards and why the real compile succeeded. A check that had trusted that message would have declared Phase E blocked on a machine that builds. The `commit` field names ea9f06b, the commit that contains the fix; the follow-up 3af0a3e only corrected the fleet line in environment.md, and pointing the field at it made the task unbacked for one verification run — caught by AUDIT/verify-done-commits.sh, which is the check that exists for exactly this.

tasks.title: The acceptance script's coverage step hardcodes the pre-Swift-6.4 test-bundle path, which no longer exists, so Phase E's coverage gate fails on the new toolchain
tasks.discovered_by: Phase A baseline, while locating the coverage profile under the new build layout
tasks.evidence_before: phase-e.sh builds `binary="$bin/ChatBotsPackageTests.xctest/Contents/MacOS/ChatBotsPackageTests"`. Under Xcode 27 / Swift 6.4 the test bundle is `ChatBotsCoreTests.xctest` with executable `Contents/MacOS/ChatBotsCoreTests`; verified: `[ -f "$bin/ChatBotsPackageTests.xctest/Contents/MacOS/ChatBotsPackageTests" ]` -> missing, while `ChatBotsCoreTests.xctest/Contents/MacOS/ChatBotsCoreTests` exists and is executable. The profile path itself (`$bin/codecov/default.profdata`) is unchanged. The step therefore fails with `coverage: no profile or no test binary` and would block Phase E for a reason that is not about the code.

The failure message now names both the profile and the bundle directory.
tasks.evidence_after: The hardcoded path does not exist and the bundles that do are visible in the evidence (`AUDIT/baseline/swift64/a134-a146-coverage.log`): `ls -d $bin/ChatBotsPackageTests.xctest` gives "No such file or directory" while `ls -d $bin/*.xctest` lists `ChatBotsAppTests.xctest` and `ChatBotsCoreTests.xctest`. After the change, `bash tools/audit-checks.sh` passes **all six** gates for the first time under this toolchain, exit 0, with `PASS  coverage: TOTAL 6085 2696 55.69% …` — 19 419 lines of `Sources/` — and `PASS  tests: 857 tests in 149 suites`. The report's larger file set is the application target being attributed for the first time: summed per target from the same log, `ChatBotsCore` is 10 994 lines at 83.61% (the baseline's 83.59%, unchanged) and `ChatBotsApp` is 8 425 lines at 1.65%, so the package figure moves from 77.08% to 55.69% because the denominator changed, not the code.
tasks.notes: Fixed as one task because A146 recorded that A134 named only the `phase-e.sh` copy and that the same assumption existed in both; leaving one behind would have left the CI gate failing on a green tree. The evidence log's first version carried a table that read the function columns instead of the line columns — 1 501 and 870 where the figures are 10 994 and 8 425 — which contradicted the prose beside it and was corrected in 394fe33; the wrong table stands in 487108d, per §0. Also worth recording for whoever reads the coverage number next: the gate has no floor by design, so the move from 77.08% to 55.69% is not a failure, and the honest way to read it is per target — the app target is mostly SwiftUI view code that has no tests, and the stores the app tests do cover read 63.83% and 63.57%.

tasks.file_line: tools/make-app.sh:89-90 and 141, tools/fetch-metal.sh (the whole strategy), Package.resolved (mlx-swift 0.31.6)
tasks.title: The repository states that mlx-swift's SwiftPM build does not compile the Metal kernels; under Xcode 27 it does, so the 190 MB separate metallib download is of unverified necessity and the stated reason for it is now false
tasks.discovered_by: Phase A baseline, from the CompileMetalFile step that failed for want of the toolchain
tasks.evidence_before: tools/make-app.sh:89-90 says: "MLX's default.metallib is fetched separately, because mlx-swift's SwiftPM build does not compile the Metal kernels (see tools/fetch-metal.sh)". Under Xcode 27 the SwiftPM build DOES compile them: the failed build stopped at `CompileMetalFile .../steel_attention.metal`, and a successful build now produces 27 artefacts under `.build/out/Intermediates.noindex/mlx-swift.build/Debug/mlx-swift_Cmlx-b.build/Metal/` (`.air`, `.dat`, `.dia`) plus `.build/out/Products/Debug/mlx-swift_Cmlx.bundle/Contents/Resources/default.metallib`. `make-app.sh` both copies that SwiftPM resource bundle into the app and installs the separately fetched `mlx.metallib` into `Contents/MacOS/`, so the shipped app may carry two Metal libraries whose relationship is unstated. tasks.title: No Origin/Referer check and Content-Type is ignored, so any web page the user visits can drive the engine; /api/seat lets it repoint a cloud seat and exfiltrate a conversation
tasks.discovered_by: Phase B audit pass (Swift 6.4 re-audit)
tasks.evidence_before: `HTTPRequest.json()` (HTTPServer.swift:41-44) decodes the body regardless of Content-Type, and no route checks Origin/Referer/Sec-Fetch-*. A page can therefore POST JSON with `Content-Type: text/plain` to 127.0.0.1:7789 — a CORS simple request, no preflight — and have it execute: /api/conversations/delete, /api/start, /api/attachments. /api/seat (APIServer.swift:630-639) accepts baseURL/apiKey/apiModel/backend from that unauthenticated body and EngineService.swift:161 stores them unvalidated, so the page can point a cloud seat at a host it controls and start a run: conversation exfiltration, not merely LAN exposure. Distinct from A01 (LAN reachability) and A75 (CORS `*`): removing the ACAO header stopped response reads, not side effects. Chrome's Private Network Access preflight may mitigate; Safari and Firefox do not send it.
tasks.fix_summary: State-changing requests must be same-origin JSON: `Origin` is checked first (a mismatch with the addressed host, taken from `X-Forwarded-Host` when Caddy is in front, is refused 403 whatever the body), then `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` is refused, then `Content-Type` must be `application/json` (415). A client that sends no Origin — curl, the CLI, a script — is unaffected, and a same-origin browser request carries an Origin matching `X-Forwarded-Host`.
tasks.evidence_after: Verified against a live engine (`chatbots-cli --serve --seed`) with curl: `Content-Type: text/plain` -> 415 with the topic unchanged; `application/json` with `Origin: http://evil.example` -> 403 with the topic unchanged; the same JSON POST with no Origin -> 200 with the topic changed. Five tests in `AuditS0CrossOriginTests`, three of which fail before the fix. Full suite 832 tests in 141 suites green; swiftlint 255 and authored swift-format 744 at their waivers; ruff, pyright, gitleaks and osv unchanged. ASan/TSan not re-run (Phase E's job; the change is codegen-neutral).
tasks.notes: The first commit of this fix (8d3fa2b) claimed in its message that the analyzers were 'exactly at their recorded waivers' when they were 256 and 748 — the new test file had added one large_tuple and four OrderedImports/AddLines findings. A store the old remove-then-move path already damaged is repaired on load by reading the stranded `conversations.json.tmp` (`readTemporary`), so an affected user recovers the history instead of being told it is empty.

The recovery test is the discriminating one: it FAILS before the fix (`load().map(\.topic)` returned `[]` for a store holding only its temporary) and passes after. tasks.title: The certificate store treats any read failure as first run, hardcodes RSA-2048 without checking the pair, executes user-writable openssl paths, and drains pipes in an order that can deadlock

tasks.discovered_by: Phase B audit pass (Swift 6.4 re-audit)

Because a passing test proves little on its own, the same evidence file records a mutation: making `token` replace the text instead of appending fails `token fragments accumulate in order` with `got "lo"`, and reverting it passes. The full suite is 844 tests in 145 suites green (`test-after-a165.log`), `tools/embed-web.py --check` passes so the served bytes and `web/` agree, and swiftlint and authored swift-format are unchanged at their waivers. What this does **not** include is a browser: no headless page was driven, so what is proven is the merge and the wiring, not a rendered frame.
tasks.notes: The check was deliberately given a home in `tools/audit-checks.sh` rather than left as a script nobody runs — an unrun test is the defect A167 records, and adding it as gate 6 is what makes it a gate. That edit also renumbered the five existing gates from /5 to /6 and added `node` to the required tools, so the script now exits 2 rather than failing obscurely on a Mac without Node. The merge was put in its own file for the same reason `TextZoom` was in A167: logic inside a page is logic nothing can run. `web/index.html` loads it before `app.js`, the embedder carries it as `/deltas.js`, the Caddy comment that enumerates what that block serves now names it, and the byte-for-byte drift test covers it so the two copies cannot diverge.

tasks.title: The transport gate leaks on cancellation, so a cancelled test permanently blocks every later transport suite
tasks.discovered_by: Phase B audit pass (Swift 6.4 re-audit)
tasks.evidence_before: `acquire()` parks on `await withCheckedContinuation { waiting.append($0) }` with no cancellation handler: a test cancelled while waiting orphans its continuation, `busy` stays true and no later suite can acquire. Throw and return paths release correctly; cancellation is the unhandled one, and a hung suite would look like a product hang.
tasks.fix_summary: `acquire()` registers a `withTaskCancellationHandler` and, when cancelled, leaves the queue through a new `abandon(_:)` and throws `CancellationError` instead of parking forever. `provideScope` takes the gate with `try await`, so cancellation propagates instead of being swallowed. The hand-over/`abandon` race is closed in `acquire`: if the gate arrives in the same instant as the cancellation, it is released before throwing. All state stays inside the actor — no `@unchecked Sendable`.
tasks.evidence_after: Against the original implementation (its body verbatim, plus read-only `isHeld`/`waitingCount` accessors so the same tests compile) the suite records 3 failing expectations in 8 ms — `waitingCount == 0` on both tests and `!held` on the first (`AUDIT/baseline/swift64/a168-before-assertions.log`) — and with the awaiting steps left in, the run never completes: it deadlocks until the 150 s timeout kills it, exit 124, with no test output at all, which is the symptom A168 reports (`a168-before-hang.log`). After the change the suite passes, and in the full suite the 2 new tests bring it to 838 tests in 143 suites green (`test-after-a168.log`). swiftlint 255 and authored swift-format 747, both unchanged from before this task with no new finding; the single `warning:` line is SwiftPM's mlx-swift_Cmlx packaging notice; §0's forbidden-construct grep over tracked Swift is empty. ASan/TSan deferred to Phase E.
tasks.notes: Correction, recorded because commit 18d4017 states it wrongly: its message says "all 4 tests pass" when the suite has 2 tests, as its own evidence line reports. This is the third instance of this audit's recurring defect — a commit message asserting a state the artifact does not have (A136 twice, now here) — and this time the artifact and the message were in the same commit and still disagreed. The commit stands: §0 forbids rewriting history, and the corrected statement is this ledger entry. The discriminating run needed a bounded variant of the tests because Swift Testing prints nothing until a run completes, so a deadlocked before-run shows no failures at all; the bounded variant and the hang are both kept as evidence, and neither is the test that ships.

tasks.title: Twenty-one teardowns are fire-and-forget tasks, so the serialising gate is released before QUIC teardown finishes and the A102 collision is reduced rather than removed
tasks.discovered_by: Phase B audit pass (Swift 6.4 re-audit)
tasks.evidence_before: `defer { Task { await running.stop() } }` returns immediately; `provideScope` then releases the gate while the previous engine's listener is still closing, which is exactly the overlap the trait exists to prevent (the recorded symptom is Network.framework's `Fatal error: Neither nw nor nwGroup is initialized`). The serialisation therefore hides a harness defect rather than proving the product safe.
tasks.fix_summary: New `TransportTeardown` (`@MainActor` registry: `register`, `drain`, `pendingCount`) in the test target, and `TransportSerialized.withGate` holds the sequence acquire → body → drain → release, used by `provideScope` and by the tests directly. tasks.title: Child output is unbounded and the conversion timeout cannot fire while output flows
tasks.discovered_by: Phase B core pass (L2/L3/L5), Swift 6.4 re-audit
tasks.evidence_before: `drain` loops on `read(descriptor, …)` and exits only on EOF/EAGAIN; a child that keeps the 64 KB pipe full — a compressed .docx/.rtf expanding to gigabytes under textutil — makes read() return >0 forever, so the outer deadline is never reached and `outputData` grows without bound. Reachable from POST /api/attachments; the 64 MiB cap applies to the input only.
tasks.fix_summary: `drain` takes a `limit` and returns as soon as it is reached, discarding what arrived in the same read, so it always returns and the poll loop always regains control. `SystemProcess.run` takes `maximumOutputBytes` (default 64 MiB, the attachment ceiling) and `TextutilExtractor` passes `limits.maximumFileBytes`; stdout past it kills and reaps the child and fails as `unreadable`, stderr past it is left unread so the child blocks and the deadline ends it. The poll loop moved into `collectOutput`.
tasks.evidence_after: `AuditS1ProcessOutputTests` runs a child that writes 64 KB every 10 ms and never ends, so the pipe keeps refilling. Against the original `drain` the 1 MB ceiling is ignored: the run accumulates ~32 MB and ends at the 5 s deadline reporting the timeout instead, which is the wrong reason and the unreachable deadline in one measurement (`AUDIT/baseline/swift64/a197-before.log`). After the change the same call stops at the ceiling in 0.35 s with `the conversion produced more than 1 MB of text`, and a second test with a 64 MB ceiling still has the deadline end the child at 1.09 s (`a197-after.log`), so the ceiling did not replace the deadline. The full suite is 841 tests in 145 suites green (`test-after-a197.log`). swiftlint 255 and authored swift-format 747, unchanged with no new finding: the `function_body_length` violation the first version produced was fixed by extracting `collectOutput`, not waived. §0 forbidden-construct grep over tracked Swift is empty.
tasks.notes: The ceiling is the same number the input is capped at, which is not a coincidence: the image path already refuses a conversion that grew past `limits.maximumFileBytes` for the reason given there, that the converted bytes travel base64-encoded in one protocol message. The text path had no such check, so this closes a gap between two paths that make the same promise. The second test passes before and after the fix and is kept as a guard rather than as discrimination: with a slow writer `drain` returns on EAGAIN, so the deadline was always reachable on that path, and what it pins is that bounding the read did not make the deadline unreachable. stderr past the ceiling is deliberately left unread rather than drained and discarded: the child then blocks on a full pipe and the deadline ends it, which bounds memory and time together.

tasks.title: A session accepted during stop() is orphaned and keeps serving
tasks.discovered_by: Phase B core pass (L2/L3/L5), Swift 6.4 re-audit
tasks.evidence_before: The accept loop checks cancellation only at the top: `while !Task.isCancelled { let session = try await listener.acceptSession(); … }`. `stop()` clears both tables, cancels the tracked tasks and then awaits `session.close()`, suspending the @MainActor — the cancelled loop resumes, inserts the new session into the cleared tables and spawns a serve task nothing cancels or closes.
tasks.fix_summary: `stop()` increments a `generation` counter before it suspends, `start()` captures it for the loop it spawns, and `acceptLoop(generation:)` re-checks both `Task.isCancelled` and the generation after every `acceptSession()` returns. A session that arrives too late is closed by the loop that accepted it, since nothing else knows it exists. The loop also stops instead of clearing the tables of a later `start()`.
tasks.evidence_after: The new `AuditS1StopRaceTests` connects six clients so that `stop()` spends a measurable time in its close loop, then starts a seventh connecting into that window. Against the original implementation the test fails in 0.33 s on both assertions — `liveSessionCount` is 1 after `stop()` returns, and the late client's `state()` returns a full snapshot, so an orphaned session was demonstrably still being served on a stopped server (`AUDIT/baseline/swift64/a198-before.log`). After the change the same test passes in 0.33 s (`a198-after.log`) and the full suite is 839 tests in 144 suites green (`test-after-a198.log`). swiftlint 255 and authored swift-format 747, both unchanged with no new finding — the two OrderedImports findings the first format run produced were fixed in the same commit rather than waived. `WebTransportSessionTests.swift` now imports `ChatBotsCore` with `@testable` so the test can read `liveSessionCount`, an internal accessor added with its reason. §0 forbidden-construct grep over tracked Swift is empty.
tasks.notes: The `liveSessionCount` accessor is the one piece of production code that exists for the test. It is internal rather than public, it reads a dictionary the class already owns, and it is what makes the invariant assertable without a timing assumption: "no session is owned after stop() returns" is true or false regardless of which side of the race the accept landed on. The generation counter was chosen over checking `listener == nil` because `start()` can run again after a `stop()`, and a loop belonging to the old listener must not register sessions into the tables the new one owns.

A136 refuses it explicitly and names the reason, so the property ('a cross-origin write gains nothing') is unchanged and strictly stronger; the `!= 204` and no-CORS-header assertions beside it are untouched.
tasks.evidence_after: `AuditS1CORSTests` passes and the whole suite is green (832/141). Recorded as its own task because §0 requires a genuinely wrong check to be fixed as a numbered task with justification rather than edited inside the fix it relates to.

tasks.title: The Phase E gate accepts only audit/2026-09-13 or main, so it fails on the branch this re-audit is developed on and the acceptance run cannot pass
tasks.discovered_by: Phase C — found by running the re-audit branch against its own gates, not by reading the ledger
tasks.evidence_before: `AUDIT/phase-e.sh:76-79` is `case "$branch" in audit/2026-09-13) pass ... ;; main) pass ... ;; *) fail "on branch '$branch', which is neither the audit branch nor main" ;; esac`. The current branch is `audit/2026-09-15` (user decision: main stays untouched until Phase E passes), so the identity check fails before any other section runs and the script exits non-zero. This is the same file and the same case arm as A132, which added `main` for exactly this reason one audit earlier — the list of acceptable branches was updated for the landing but not for the next audit, so the gate is once again wrong about the branch the audit is developed on.
tasks.fix_summary: The branch is matched as `audit/*` instead of by the date it was cut, and the result names the branch it found. `main` is unchanged.
tasks.evidence_after: Section 0 of the real script now prints `PASS  on the audit branch 'audit/2026-09-15', where the audit was developed` on this branch, followed by PASS on sections 1/12 and 2/12 (`/tmp/phase-e-a210.log`; the run was stopped at 90 s on purpose, because the remaining sections are the acceptance run itself and belong on the fresh Phase E host). The case pattern was exercised directly against four branch names, old vs new: `audit/2026-09-13` PASS/PASS, `audit/2026-09-15` **FAIL/PASS**, `main` PASS/PASS, `feature/x` FAIL/FAIL — so the change widens acceptance to audit branches only and the control still fails. `shellcheck AUDIT/phase-e.sh` clean; swiftlint still 255 with no new finding.
tasks.notes: This is the second time this exact case arm has been wrong, both times because the list was written for the audit in front of it: A132 added `main` after the landing, and this adds the shape `audit/*` so the next audit date does not have to remember to edit a gate it has not read yet. The branch is now named in the pass line, so the evidence still records which branch was verified rather than merely that one was.

tasks.title: The session entry point still says the audit is complete and names the landed 2026-09-13 branch, while 73 findings are open on a different, unmerged branch
tasks.discovered_by: Phase C — noticed while checking the branch references the new findings turned up
tasks.evidence_before: `HANDOVER.md:3` says "**The audit is complete.**" and its state table says "127 enumerated: 127 DONE, 0 open, 0 BLOCKED" with "Phases E green". `HANDOVER.md:14` and `ledger.md:6` both say the branch is `audit/2026-09-13`, cut from `main@a6d6999`, and that branch and `main` "point at the same commit". The state on disk is: 209 tasks with 136 DONE and 73 open (9 S1), on `audit/2026-09-15` cut from `main@02ddd4e`, with `main` at `349fefe` — so the two do not point at the same commit, Phase E has not been run for this audit, and the branch is deliberately unmerged. `plan.md:144` still states the commit convention as being on `audit/2026-09-13`. A118 recorded this same defect class for `ledger.md` (it was called the source of truth and stopped at A89); the prose was fixed then but the header and the handover were not, and the re-audit re-created the condition because `HANDOVER.md` describes the previous audit as if it were the current one.
tasks.fix_summary: `HANDOVER.md` leads with the current re-audit (branch, severity, toolchain, phases, entry point) and labels everything below as the landed 2026-09-13 audit history; it carries no task count, pointing at the generated table in `ledger.md` instead. `ledger.md:6`, `plan.md:6,145` and `inventory.md:3` now state the branch this work is on and that it is not the same commit as `main`.
tasks.evidence_after: Re-read the four documents against the repository state. `grep -rn` for the completion claims now matches only HANDOVER.md:3, which states the opposite (\"The 2026-09-13 audit is complete and landed. The 2026-09-15 re-audit is not.\"), plus the A211 row in the generated ledger tables. No tracked file still asserts that this branch and `main` are the same commit (`git grep -n \"same commit\" AUDIT/`), and `git rev-parse` agrees with what the documents now say: branch `audit/2026-09-15`, merge-base `02ddd4e`, `origin/main` `349fefe`. `AUDIT/render-ledger.sh --check` passes after the edit, so the hand-written header did not disturb the generated region. The counts the entry point used to carry are now pointed at rather than copied, which is the property that makes this not recur.
tasks.notes: This is A118 one audit later, and the fix is deliberately not another copied count: the handover now says where the number lives instead of repeating it. The 2026-09-13 history is kept verbatim below a clear boundary rather than rewritten, because §0 forbids rewriting history and because the reasoning in it is still the useful part.

tasks.title: Two wiki clones carried a GitHub personal access token in plaintext inside their origin URL, so the credential that can write to the wikis and to this repository sat in a readable file
tasks.discovered_by: Phase C — the post-push wiki sync check the standing instructions require after every push
tasks.evidence_before: `git -C ~/Downloads/chatbots-wiki-ro remote -v` printed the `origin` URL as `https://Pummelchen:<fine-grained-pat>@github.com/Pummelchen/ChatBots.wiki.git`, and `mcps-wiki-ro` carried the same shape for `MCPSearch.wiki.git`. Both were plaintext in `.git/config`. `aisessionserver-wiki` was clean, as were `ChatBots/.git/config` and the other repository clones. This is the credential that can push to these repositories: `gh` is logged in as `Pummelchen` from `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`, and the same helper authenticated a push of the audit branch minutes earlier. The audited repository itself is unaffected — gitleaks reported 0 findings over the full history in Phase A, and the token appears in no tracked file.
tasks.fix_summary: Both remote URLs were rewritten to the bare `https://github.com/...` form with `git remote set-url`, removing the embedded credential. `~/.gitconfig` already routes `github.com` through `gh auth git-credential`, so authentication continues to work without a secret in any URL: a fetch against the rewritten `chatbots-wiki-ro` was run afterwards and succeeded, and `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml` (mode 0600) remains the one place the token is stored.
tasks.evidence_after: `grep` for `github_pat_`/`ghp_` across `.git/config` of all six clones in `~/Downloads/` now reports clean for every one, where the same check before the fix reported two. The rewritten URLs are named in `AUDIT/environment.md` ("A credential was sitting in plaintext in two wiki clones (A212)") with the shape of what was there and what replaced it, and with the recommendation that the token be rotated: it was displayed on screen while being found, so it should be treated as disclosed even though it was never committed.
tasks.notes: Recorded rather than fixed silently, and filed even though the file is outside the tree this audit has scope over: the brief limits the audit to Pummelchen/ChatBots, so there is no repository change to point at and `verify-done-commits.sh` reports this task as skipped rather than backed. The same finding is why the ChatBots clone needed its URL fixed too — it carried a bare `Pummelchen:@` userinfo with no password, which is what made `git push` fail with "Invalid username or token" while reads (anonymous, on a public repository) kept working. That fix is also local config and is described in this entry rather than committed.

tasks.title: The DONE-commit guard recognised only .swift, .py and .sh paths, so a task fixed in the web interface or a CI workflow could be reported unbacked while its commit contained the fix
tasks.discovered_by: Phase C — the guard caught A165's ledger entry after its fix was committed, and the reason it gave was wrong
tasks.evidence_before: A165 is DONE against 3445aee, a commit whose changes include `web/app.js`, `web/deltas.js`, `web/index.html` and `Caddyfile`. Its record names `web/app.js:1426-1429; Sources/ChatBotsCore/APIServer.swift:730-746`, and the guard reported `FAIL   A165  commit 3445aee touches none of: Sources/ChatBotsCore/APIServer.swift`, with totals `backed 127 · skipped 17 · unbacked 1`. Its path extraction was `grep -oE '[A-Za-z0-9_./-]*\.(swift|py|sh)[^ ,;:)]*'`, so `web/app.js` was invisible: the guard could not see the file the fix is in, and the one path it could see is the end of the wire that did not need changing. This is the class A19, A83, A117 and A89 record — a control reporting on a claim it cannot see — and the direction matters: reporting *unbacked* rather than *unchecked* means a JavaScript-only fix had no way to be verified at all.
tasks.fix_summary: The extension list becomes `swift|py|sh|js|html|css|yml`, with the reason written where it is used and in the header, which no longer claims a CI workflow is out of scope. Four more DONE tasks became checkable.
tasks.evidence_after: `AUDIT/verify-done-commits.sh` now reports `ok     A165  3445aee touches web/app.js`, and the totals move from `backed 127 · skipped 17 · unbacked 1` to `backed 132 · skipped 13 · unbacked 0` (`AUDIT/baseline/swift64/a213-guard.log` records the old regex, the old verdict, the new regex and the new verdict). Widening it also surfaced one real record defect rather than only the false alarm it was opened for: A01 was reported unbacked because the single path the guard could see in its record, `web/app.js`, was a prose mention its commit does not touch — its fix is in the Caddyfile and the start scripts. A01's `file_line` now names `tools/start.sh` and `tools/start-web-mobile.sh`, the entry's notes record the correction, and A01 verifies as backed against `c91a310`.
tasks.notes: The temptation was to narrow the guard again so A165 passed, which would have made the check report success by looking away — the failure mode A83 and A117 both are. The list was widened instead, and the one genuine record error it exposed was corrected in the record rather than in the guard. Making the guard read only structured fields was the other option, but `file_line` is the structured field the ledger has, and its being free prose is what lets a task name a line number; the cost is that a prose mention counts, so a wrong verdict here is resolved by making the record accurate.
